articles.summary: Polymarket News Today: Fed Rate Cut or Hike After CPI, PPI Shock?  Coin Gabbar
articles.full_text:
Money moved fast this week. Traders watched two inflation reports land back to back, and Polymarket news today shows just how shaky their confidence got. One prediction market swung from calm to chaos and back again in 48 hours. The crypto market felt it too, with prices sliding as the odds flipped. Here’s exactly what happened, what the numbers say, and what the Federal Reserve might do next.
Key Takeaways
This week’s Polymarket news today centers on one simple fact: inflation refuses to cool down. The Kobeissi Letter reported that US CPI inflation climbed to 3.7%, nearly double the Fed’s 2% target. US PPI inflation jumped even higher, to 6.3%, over three times that target. Core PPI, which strips out food and energy, reached 5.0%, two and a half times the Fed’s goal.
September marked the 67th straight month that CPI inflation stayed above the Fed’s 2% target. The US dollar has lost nearly a quarter of its value over the past five years, per the same report. Numbers like these don’t just move bond yields. They move Polymarket odds too, and this one reacted within hours of each release.
The ripple reached crypto as well. CoinGecko data shows the global crypto market cap sitting at $2.83 trillion today, down 0.8% over the last 24 hours.
Source: Coingecko Data
Daily trading volume stands at $75.87 billion, while Bitcoin dominance holds at 57.7% and Ethereum dominance sits at 10.4%. Prices surged before the data, shook once the numbers hit, and are cooling off again now.
That’s the real story behind Polymarket news today: a single market called “Fed Decision in October” that moved harder than anyone expected.
Source: Official Site
| Timing | No Change Odds | 25 bps Hike Odds | 
|---|---|---|
| Before CPI & PPI (pre-Oct 15) | 80-81% | 19-20% | 
| Between CPI & PPI (Oct 15-16) | 52-72% | 28-48% | 
| After Both Reports (post-Oct 16) | 87% | 14% | 
Before the data dropped, bettors felt comfortable. No change looked like the safe bet at 80-81%. Once CPI landed, then PPI followed a day later, confidence cracked. Hike odds nearly tripled at one point, hitting 48%.
But once both reports were fully priced in, the odds snapped back toward 87% for no change and just 14% for a hike. The market shook, then steadied.
Not everyone panicked. On Polymarket’s separate “How many rate cuts in 2026” question, the odds barely moved before, during, or after the inflation reports. No rate cut held at 96.9% (roughly 97%) the entire time. A single 25 bps cut sat at just 0.8%.
Source: Official Website
Hot CPI and PPI prints shook the October decision odds, but this longer-term market shrugged them off completely.
Context matters here. The Federal Reserve hadn’t raised rates since July 2023. That changed on September 16, 2026, when the FOMC voted 12-0 to hike rates by 25 basis points, pushing the range to 3.75%-4.00%. Rates were cut back in December 2025, so September’s move was the first change in either direction since then.
That single vote is the backdrop every Polymarket bettor is now pricing against.
So where does this leave things? Polymarket’s current data points to no change at the next two meetings:
That’s the prediction today, not a guarantee. Betting markets can flip fast, as this very week proved. One more hot inflation print could reopen the hike debate before either date arrives.
Expert Opinion: Market analysts note that prediction markets like Polymarket tend to overreact to single data points before drifting back toward their baseline, a pattern visible in this week’s swing from 81% to 52% and back to 87%. The gap between hot inflation data and steady long-term rate-cut prediction suggests bettors still trust the Fed’s September hike to do its job, at least for now. Analysts add that one more hot CPI or PPI print could easily reopen the hike debate before October 28.
Polymarket news today paints a clear picture: traders expect the Fed to hold steady at its October 28 and December 9 meetings, even with inflation running hot. Prediction markets move fast, though, and nothing is locked in until they actually votes. Watch the data, not the headlines.

articles.title: UK inflation can seal the deal on BOE’s November rate hike - The Edge Malaysia
articles.summary: UK inflation can seal the deal on BOE’s November rate hike  The Edge Malaysia
articles.full_text:
(Oct 18): A pickup in UK inflation to a nine-month high in data this week is likely to set the stage for key decisions from the upcoming budget to a likely interest-rate increase.
The report on Wednesday is anticipated by economists to show annual price growth in September at 3.4%. The result will amount to a reality check for British policymakers returning to London after warm words and an upgraded growth forecast from the International Monetary Fund.
The inflation data are likely to help seal the deal on the first rate hike from the Bank of England in over three years in November, while also feeding into the thinking of Chancellor of the Exchequer John Healey, who has vowed to give businesses and households some “breathing space” at next week’s budget.
His fiscal plans are being hemmed in by the global bond rout after the resurgence in energy prices prompted traders to bet on a series of BOE rate increases to contain inflationary pressures.
Gilt yields have risen to around their highest levels in decades, eroding Healey’s already-thin fiscal wiggle room. Tax hikes are likely to be needed to fund any cost-of-living measures, with banks set to be targeted.
While the BOE has held off on raising borrowing costs so far, investors are betting on it joining the Federal Reserve and European Central Bank in tightening policy at its upcoming meeting on Nov 5.
“The combination of soaring inflation, resilient demand and a stabilising labour market will make it hard for the BOE to remain on hold. We expect a 25-basis-point hike at the central bank’s next meeting in November. We also see another move in February,” said Bloomberg Economics.
Governor Andrew Bailey said in Bangkok last week that there is little evidence the energy shock is spreading widely across the economy yet, and figures on Tuesday will also likely suggest that price pressures from the labor market remain muted.
But the inflation situation is predicted to get worse. Bailey warned that the longer the Middle East conflict drags on, the more difficult it’s becoming to avoid a hike. The UK central bank is already forecasting that inflation will top 4% in early 2027, double its 2% target.
Elsewhere, Chinese growth data, Japanese inflation, global purchasing manager indexes and a rate decision from the embattled Indonesian central bank may be among the highlights.
Below is our wrap of what is coming up in the global economy.
In the wake of fresh inflation figures that showed price pressures are accelerating, the US economic data calendar lightens up. On Tuesday, separate reports on new residential construction and pending sales of previously owned homes are projected to illustrate the housing market was still struggling for traction in September.
Affordability constraints continue to weigh on demand, with 30-year mortgage rates recently hitting an almost three-year high of 7.5%.
On Friday, S&P Global will release its preliminary October manufacturing and services indexes. Economists see both measures pointing to solid growth, yet at a slightly slower pace. The same day, the University of Michigan releases its final October consumer sentiment reading.
Federal Reserve policymakers are in a media blackout period ahead of the Oct 27-28 policy meeting.
In Canada, Monday’s inflation update and business outlook will provide the final major clues to how the economy is weathering oil-driven inflation risks and the fallout from escalating trade tensions before policymakers make their next rate decision on Oct 28.
Headline yearly change in the consumer price index has held near 3% for months, which Bank of Canada governor Tiff Macklem has called “too high.” Economists expect it accelerated in September to 3.2%, though core measures likely held steady.
Meanwhile, retail sales likely rebounded in August after a temporary slump in July, though the resurgence may be short lived.
Albertans will vote Monday in a referendum that asks whether they’d like to begin a process to separate from Canada. The “remain” side holds a comfortable lead, but federalists fear high turnout for separation will introduce political and economics risks.
Later in the week, Prime Minister Mark Carney will travel to Türkiye to advance talks for a comprehensive trade agreement.
China releasing key economic data and several central banks lining up monetary policy decisions take the spotlight in Asia-Pacific this week.
China releases its third-quarter gross domestic product alongside September retail sales, industrial production, fixed-asset investment and property data on Monday. The figures will show the economic momentum in the world’s second-largest economy amid a prolonged property downturn that continues to weigh on investment.
China’s one-year and five-year loan prime rates on Tuesday are expected to stay unchanged at 3% and 3.5%, respectively. Industrial production data due Monday will also help gauge manufacturing activity in the country.
Indonesia is expected to keep its policy rate unchanged at 5.75% on Wednesday, while the Philippines is seen raising 25 basis points on Thursday. Rate-hike pressures prevail in South Korea too. The decisions will be closely watched as officials across the region balance inflation and currency pressures against risks to growth.
Inflation and business activity put Japan in focus on Friday. National CPI will offer another indication of whether price pressures remain strong enough to support the Bank of Japan’s historic policy-normalisation path.
Japan’s flash PMIs the same day will show whether growth remains broad-based across manufacturing and services. Trade data on Wednesday will provide another gauge of external demand.
Flash PMIs are also due in India that day. They will be closely watched for signs of how the economy is coping with a difficult external environment as inflation firms and oil prices remain above US$100 (RM408) a barrel. Core industries output, due Wednesday, will provide an earlier read on industrial momentum.
Elsewhere, South Korea’s early trade data and Taiwan’s export orders will help investors assess the strength of the regional trade and technology cycle.
Reserve Bank of Australia assistant governor Christopher Kent is due for an interview on News24 on Sunday and a fireside chat on Monday. RBA deputy governor Andrew Hauser is due to make an appearance on Wednesday.
Germany’s ZEW investor confidence survey is due on Tuesday. The euro region’s first PMIs from the final quarter of the year will be a highlight, with those numbers on Friday seen likely to show resilient expansion. The European Central Bank’s survey of consumer expectations comes out the same day.
Few policymakers are on the calendar after last week’s IMF meetings, and a blackout period in advance of the Oct 29 rate decision will kick in on Wednesday.
France will continue to draw attention for its extended budget troubles. The country has been on negative outlook at Moody’s Ratings for a year, raising the prospect that a review result scheduled for Friday will lead to a downgrade.
Away from the eurozone, Hungary is due to unveil its 2027 budget at the start of the week, giving first concrete indications of how it plans to more than halve its deficit to the 3% required to join by the euro.
Meanwhile on Thursday, the Swiss National Bank will publish a summary of its September decision, when officials kept borrowing costs unchanged while dialling down their threat of franc intervention.
In South Africa, data on Wednesday will likely show inflation accelerated in September as fuel prices continue to climb.
Later in the day, Finance Minister Enoch Godongwana will present his medium-term budget in Cape Town, with investors looking for signs of commitment to repairing the public finances through a fiscal anchor. They also expect progress on consolidation, helped by mining-tax revenue and a narrower-than-expected deficit.
A number of monetary decisions are scheduled:
The August GDP-proxy report from Argentina will likely add fresh evidence that the economy is on track to enter a technical recession, which would be the second under President Javier Milei.
Local economists now forecast third-quarter output at -1% — down from a forecast of 1.1% growth just a month ago — in the wake of July’s GDP-proxy report that showed the economy taking its steepest tumble since April 2020.
In Colombia, August’s 7.4-magnitude quake that struck the western part of the country will weigh heavily on the month’s economic activity data. Extensive damage from the temblor is expected to damp growth into 2027 before rebuilding gives the economy a boost.
Mexico offers up myriad growth indicators in the coming week, with GDP-proxy figures, joblessness and retail sales, which are likely to underscore the economy’s resilience.
Early October consumer prices data — the last inflation figures policymakers will get before their Nov 5 rate decision — aren’t likely to alarm or assure Banxico’s board.
Paraguay’s central bank has been on hold since a quarter-point cut in February put the key rate at 5.5%. Annual inflation ticked up to 1.7% in September though policymakers project it ending the year near the 3.5% center of their target range.
Rounding out the week in economic reports, Brazil on Friday publishes its mid-October consumer prices report ahead of Sunday’s presidential run-off election. Polling shows that the race has tightened up, but Senator Flávio Bolsonaro still appears poised to deny President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva his bid for a fourth term.
On the inflation front, the early consensus sees the annual print rising beyond the 4.5% ceiling of the central bank’s target range, perhaps nearing 4.8.
Economists in the central bank’s Oct 9 survey raised their 2026 inflation estimate for Latin America’s biggest economy to 5.22%, a 21 basis-point rise over the previous survey.

articles.summary: BOJ Chief Rules Out Inflation Above 2%, Signals More Rate Hikes  Seoul Economic Daily
articles.full_text:
Bank of Japan Governor Kazuo Ueda said the central bank will not tolerate underlying inflation running above its 2% target and will press ahead with interest rate increases.
Ueda made the remarks at a news conference on the 16th in Bangkok, where finance ministers and central bank governors of the Group of 20 were meeting, according to the Nihon Keizai Shimbun, Reuters and other foreign media on the 17th.
"Underlying inflation is broadly close to our 2% target, so we cannot tolerate it rising further," Ueda said. "Our policy stance has recently shifted into a phase in which anchoring inflation near the 2% target becomes an important policy goal." On financial conditions, Ueda said the environment has remained accommodative even after last month's rate increase, adding that the central bank "will continue to adjust the degree of easing by raising the policy rate." He said the BOJ would review the issue at its next monetary policy meeting.
The comments came ahead of a key BOJ monetary policy meeting later this month. Board members will present new quarterly projections for growth and prices at the gathering, which markets are expected to scrutinize for clues on the pace and timing of further rate increases. At last month's meeting, the BOJ raised its short-term policy rate, the benchmark, by 0.25 percentage points to about 1.25% from about 1.0%.
Financial markets largely expect the BOJ to hold rates steady at this month's meeting, with attention turning to whether it will deliver another increase at its December gathering, the Nikkei reported. Reuters, citing sources, said many within the central bank favor keeping rates unchanged at the meeting later this month and waiting for more data showing how the increases so far have affected the economy and financial conditions, while adding that the BOJ is expected to send hawkish signals leaving the door open to a December hike.

ECB officials see December rate hike as uncertainty clouds 2027 outlook
Policymakers see December as the likeliest time for a rate increase, while rising bond yields, high energy costs, AI investment and uncertainty over US policy complicate the outlook for next year
European Central Bank officials are preparing to finish 2026 with a third interest-rate increase, the last before an increasingly complex backdrop overshadows decisions next year.
While policymakers speaking this week in Bangkok kept open the option of acting in October, they pointed to December as the more likely timing for a hike that’s also widely anticipated among traders and economists.
But the discussions also revealed growing unease over issues including rising bond yields, high energy costs and the blistering investment boom in artificial intelligence.
“The tradeoffs for monetary policy are going to get more tricky,” Governing Council member Martins Kazaks said in an interview. “So far, the decisions have been relatively easy. But there’s a lot of uncertainty and very low visibility.”
The gathering in the Thai capital was dominated by warnings that the economy’s surprising resilience to the Middle East conflict will come under increasing strain. The euro zone, where investors have pushed up France’s borrowing costs due to its gaping budget deficit and political gridlock, was a focal point.
US midterm elections and an unpredictable response from President Donald Trump are adding to the uncertainty.
Policymakers signaled a preference for sticking with a quarterly pace of rate increases, suggesting continuity after being the first major central bank to hike rates since the war broke out. That would mean waiting until the Dec. 17 gathering, when they’ll have new economic forecasts.
“From a policymaker’s perspective, you want to take decisions when you have the largest amount of data available, and the next such meeting is December,” Governing Council member Gediminas Simkus said in a separate interview. “But you also can’t ignore the fact that we have a meeting in October.”
On the bright side, the Lithuanian and his colleagues pointed out that inflation heading toward 4 per cent — double the ECB’s target — hasn’t yet spread widely. At the same time, there are no signs that energy-driven price pressures are letting up.
On Friday, Brent oil hit $110 a barrel for the first time since May after Iran-backed Houthi rebels pummeled Saudi Arabia with missile and drone strikes, and Russia and Ukraine exchanged tit-for-tat attacks on energy infrastructure.
With wage negotiations looming next spring, the ECB is carefully analyzing how such shocks are “traveling through the economy,” President Christine Lagarde told CNN. “We are not seeing any of that yet, but we have to be extremely careful that little signs, indices of such secondary effects are visible.”
Officials are already pondering how restrictive monetary policy needs to become. The last two hikes, in June and September, took the deposit rate to the upper end of the range the ECB previously identified as neutral.
Additional moves — traders are betting on three by September next year — would start to damp economic activity just as a long-awaited recovery is taking hold.
“The market is pricing that we are going to have to do more,” Governing Council member Pierre Wunsch told Bloomberg TV. “It’s a base case that looks reasonable, but again, we are in a very uncertain world.”
Some of that uncertainty is originating in Europe, with French finances in the spotlight after a bond-market selloff stoked memories of the sovereign-debt crisis that shook the region through much of the 2010s.
Many participants in Bangkok, including IMF chief Kristalina Georgieva, argued that large budget deficits and debts must urgently be addressed, calling advanced economies the “worst offenders.”
While some ECB officials signaled optimism that the message investors sent to France has resonated with the government as it prepares key budget votes, others are already focused on how to respond if the situation deteriorates.
“The toolbox allows for quite a lot of instruments,” said Governing Council member Martin Kocher. “We are not at the stage where we need to discuss any of these instruments. But they are there if they are needed.”
The ECB’s work is overshadowed by increasing frustration among officials about Lagarde’s refusal to offer clarity on a possible early exit, according to people familiar with the matter.
The institution is in the midst of a major leadership overhaul, with Executive Board member Isabel Schnabel leaving in January, Chief Economist Philip Lane’s term expiring in May and Lagarde’s technically running through October 2027. Vice President Boris Vujcic joined in June.

articles.title: Crude Oil Market Update: WTI Backwardation and Demand Downgrades - CMB News
articles.summary: Crude Oil Market Update: WTI Backwardation and Demand Downgrades  CMB News
articles.full_text:
WTI near $97.60 and Brent around $105 show steep backwardation as tight prompt supply collides with weaker 2026 demand forecasts and softening diesel cracks.
Prices & Term Structure
The front WTI contract for November 2026 settled at 97.60 USD/bbl on 15 October, gaining 2.51 USD or 2.57% versus the previous day, extending the rebound from September’s sharp sell‑off. Brent December 2026 closed at 105.64 USD/bbl, down 0.42 USD (‑0.40%) on the day, highlighting a modest divergence: WTI rallied on U.S. inventory draws while Brent eased on softer demand headlines. Across the WTI curve, prices decline from 97.60 USD/bbl (Nov 2026) and 96.17 USD/bbl (Dec 2026) to around 78–80 USD/bbl in early 2028 and further down toward roughly 54–56 USD/bbl by late 2033 and about 50–51 USD/bbl by 2036–2037. Brent displays an even higher prompt premium, sliding from 105.64 USD/bbl (Dec 2026) to the low‑60s USD/bbl by 2035–2037. ICE Low‑Sulfur Gas Oil mirrors the crude backwardation but from a much higher outright level. The front November 2026 contract ended at 1,421.75 USD/t (‑1.86% d/d), with a consistent downward slope through the late‑2020s and early‑2030s, indicating expectations of a gradual normalisation from today’s exceptionally tight distillate market.
| Contract | Settlement (USD) | D/d change (USD) | D/d change (%) | 
|---|---|---|---|
| WTI Nov 2026 | 97.60 / bbl | +2.51 | +2.57% | 
| WTI Dec 2026 | 96.17 / bbl | +2.27 | +2.36% | 
| Brent Dec 2026 | 105.64 / bbl | -0.42 | -0.40% | 
| Gasoil Nov 2026 | 1,421.75 / t | -26.50 | -1.86% | 
Supply, Demand & Geopolitics
The IEA’s October Oil Market Report now projects global oil demand in 2026 falling by about 2.6 million bbl/d year‑on‑year, revising down earlier expectations and attributing the decline to high prices, war‑related disruptions and a softening macro backdrop. OPEC has likewise trimmed its demand outlook, underlining a rare consensus on weaker consumption into 2026. On the supply side, the IEA still expects market balances to remain in deficit through the end of 2026, as curtailed Middle East flows, infrastructure damage and refinery maintenance keep effective supply below potential. U.S. EIA data show an 8.6 million bbl draw in U.S. commercial crude stocks in the week ending 9 October, taking inventories down to roughly 416 million bbl and reinforcing the perception of tight prompt availability. Regional disruptions continue to shape sentiment. Ongoing conflict involving Iran and repeated drone attacks on shipping in the Gulf region have raised perceived risk premia, especially for Brent‑linked grades, while the rebound in Saudi exports from onshore storage acts as a partial offset. In the U.S. Gulf, Hurricane Isaias has led to limited platform evacuations so far, with only about 1% of manned production platforms shut‑in, implying a relatively minor direct production impact at this stage but adding to short‑term volatility.
Curve Shape & Product Markets
The WTI and Brent forward curves reveal exceptionally steep backwardation over the next 24–36 months. For WTI, the spread between Nov 2026 (97.60 USD/bbl) and Dec 2029 (66.90 USD/bbl) exceeds 30 USD, and the decline from front‑month to early‑2030s exceeds 40 USD. Brent shows a similar pattern, sliding from 105.64 USD/bbl (Dec 2026) toward around 61–62 USD/bbl by 2035. Such a structure signals:
- Strong preference for prompt barrels, incentivising destocking and discouraging storage builds.
- Market expectations that current geopolitical and logistical constraints will ease over the medium term.
- Growing confidence that structural demand growth will be weaker in the 2030s, in line with the IEA’s more subdued long‑term scenarios.
Distillate markets remain a key driver. Despite slightly softer gasoil futures on 15 October (front month down around 1.9%), the IEA highlights that middle distillate supplies are likely to remain constrained into 2027, with global gasoil exports roughly 10% below year‑earlier levels over the first nine months of 2026. This keeps refinery margins for diesel rich and provides a floor for crude runs, even as gasoline cracks soften seasonally.
Weather & Short‑Term Physical Outlook
Tropical activity in the Gulf of Mexico remains an operational watchpoint. Hurricane Isaias has triggered precautionary shutdowns and limited evacuations, but current federal assessments indicate only a small share of platforms affected and no major infrastructure damage reported yet. Given the steep backwardation and low visible inventories, even modest storm‑related disruptions to offshore production or refining could prompt outsized moves in prompt spreads and regional grades over the coming days. However, absent a direct hit on major refining clusters, the broader supply picture is still dominated by Middle East risks and policy‑driven stock releases rather than U.S. weather.
Trading Outlook
- Flat price: With WTI near 97–98 USD/bbl and Brent around 105 USD/bbl, upside appears increasingly headline‑driven. Inventory draws and Gulf tensions argue for resilience, but synchronised demand downgrades from IEA and OPEC limit sustained rallies much above recent highs.
- Time spreads: The pronounced backwardation from late‑2026 through 2028 favours roll‑down strategies and discourages long‑term storage plays. Front spreads should stay firm as long as U.S. stocks trend lower and Middle East supply remains fragile.
- Crude vs. products: Recent underperformance of gasoil versus crude suggests some moderation in distillate tightness, though absolute price levels remain high. Refiners with middle‑distillate‑heavy yields still benefit, but hedge ratios may need adjustment if the diesel premium continues to erode.
- Risk management: Heightened event risk around Gulf shipping lanes and hurricane season justifies maintaining optionality via options rather than leveraged directional futures positions, especially for short‑dated exposure.
3‑Day Price Direction Indication
- NYMEX WTI front month: Mildly bullish bias; tight inventories and ongoing Gulf/Middle East risks support tests of recent highs, albeit with intraday volatility around macro data and storm headlines.
- ICE Brent front month: Range‑to‑slightly‑softer; risk premium remains embedded, but repeated demand downgrades and signs of recovering exports argue for consolidation below recent peaks.
- ICE Gasoil front month: Neutral‑to‑slightly‑weaker; strong underlying fundamentals persist, yet recent corrections and expectations of incremental stock releases cap near‑term rallies.

articles.title: Is The $4B Treasury Buyback A Policy Mistake? Bessent’s Mentor Thinks Yes, But Some Say ‘Don't Fight The Treasury’ - Stocktwits
articles.summary: Is The $4B Treasury Buyback A Policy Mistake? Bessent’s Mentor Thinks Yes, But Some Say ‘Don't Fight The Treasury’  Stocktwits
articles.full_text:
Last week, the U.S. Treasury announced that it would double long-dated bond buybacks to at least $4 billion per operation, after the 30-year Treasury yield hit a 19-year high.
While the announcement briefly sent yields lower, they quickly reversed, climbing above pre-announcement levels by Aug. 20.
Stanley Druckenmiller, the American investor who also mentored Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent in his early career, suggested in an opinion piece in The Wall Street Journal that the move was a policy error.
“The market’s verdict was swift and correct: This wasn’t liquidity management, it was price management—and a mistake far larger than $4 billion suggests,” he said.
The billionaire investor and one of the most valued voices on Wall Street argued that the move didn’t justify the market’s reaction, which was simply “doing its job” even as “volatility was contained and trading was orderly.”
Druckenmiller said that the bond market’s recent weakness reflects an economy with 3%–4% inflation, 4.1% unemployment, a roughly 6% fiscal deficit and $40 trillion in debt, while the 10-year yield remains around the economy’s nominal growth rate. The bond market was only starting to push back against fiscal and inflationary pressures, he noted.
“I have spent five decades trading on a simple premise: Markets aggregate information no committee possesses, and prices are how that information reaches decision makers. The long-term Treasury yield is the most important price in the world. It is also the only fiscal disciplinarian the U.S. has left,” Druckenmiller said.
“Once markets believe Treasury is defending a price, every rise in yields becomes a test of official resolve, and the operations must grow to survive the tests,” he added.
The U.S. Treasury announced the purchase of long-dated bonds on Aug. 19 as borrowing costs soared and long-term interest rates, especially the 30-Year Treasury Yields hit their highest levels since 2007.
The Treasury department justified the move to support liquidity in the market. “This increase in buyback operation sizes reflects Treasury’s desire to provide greater liquidity support in longer-dated nominal sectors where there is consistent strong sponsorship from market participants, as evidenced by the significant volume of high-quality offers Treasury routinely receives in longer-dated buyback operations,” it said in a statement.
Mohamed El-Erian, Chief Economic Advisor at Allianz, called the buyback strategy ‘Operation Twist’ in an interview with CNBC, which would likely produce “collateral damage.”
El-Erian said Treasury’s move was tantamount to buying the long end while issuing more debt at the short end to influence yields. “So you end up messing up the short end of the curve because you want to protect the long end of the curve. That's one thing you do,” he said.
He also said that the move was driven less by economic concerns and more by political and social pressures, particularly rising mortgage and credit-card costs for lower-income households.
While yield-curve control (YCC) can provide short-term relief, he warned it would carry “collateral damage and unintended consequences,” that cannot resolve the longer-term tension between economic growth, AI investment and rising funding costs.
“So whichever way you look, these YCC measures are not a free lunch at all,” he added.
Meanwhile, The Kobeissi Letter, which provides commentary on global capital markets, justified the Treasury’s decision as a “historic intervention” amid rising bond yields.
In a post on X, the commentary service noted that despite several announcements by the U.S. Treasury intervention, yields have stayed stubborn.
“The reality is that the Fed cannot cut rates in this environment and the Trump Administration knows this. So, direct bond market intervention is the only solution to drive interest rates and yields lower over the short-run,” it said.
“Our view? Don't fight the Treasury,” it added.
The U.S. 30-Year Treasury yields were trading at 5.238% at the time of writing, edging closer to last week’s highs when it hit 5.34%. Meanwhile, the 10-year Treasury yields were trading at 4.71%, compared to a high of 4.74% last week.
The iShares 10-20 Year Treasury Bond ETF (TLH), that tracks U.S. government bonds with maturity dates between 10 and 20 years, was up 0.04% overnight amid ‘bearish’ sentiment.
The iShares 20+ Year Treasury Bond ETF (TLT) was down 0.07% amid ‘bullish’ sentiment, while iShares U.S. Treasury Bond ETF (GOVT), which is a basket of debt multiple-term securities issued by the U.S. government, was up 0.27% amid ‘neutral’ sentiment.
Meanwhile, the SPDR S&P 500 ETF (SPY), the Invesco QQQ Trust (QQQ) and the SPDR Dow Jones Industrial Average ETF Trust (DIA) were all edging higher at the time of writing.

Trump’s portfolio acquired between $15,001 and $50,000 of SpaceX shares on June 23, less than two weeks after the company’s record U.S. IPO valued it at $1.77 trillion. The transaction was one of more than 1,000 trades disclosed for June.

The stake is notable since SpaceX is a major military contractor that depends on federal approvals for its expanding launch operations.

DRAM, including high-bandwidth memory for AI, and advanced foundries should drive near-term growth, followed by NAND and logic. articles.title: Gold's Bounce Is a Bet on the Fed, Not a Verdict on Inflation - ad-hoc-news.de
articles.summary: Gold's Bounce Is a Bet on the Fed, Not a Verdict on Inflation  ad-hoc-news.de
articles.full_text:
Gold snapped a three-session losing streak on Thursday, but the rebound says more about the bond market than about any change in the inflation picture. Spot metal settled at USD 4,175.55 an ounce as Treasury yields eased and the dollar softened — the two forces that have been dictating the metal's direction all autumn.
The move higher came courtesy of Reuters, which attributed the gains to retreating US yields and a weaker greenback. What it did not signal was an all-clear on prices. Gold remains caught between a Federal Reserve that has shown little appetite for cutting and a structural bid from official-sector buyers that refuses to fade.
Rate bets wobble after a hot CPI print
Wednesday's inflation report from the US Bureau of Labor Statistics landed with a thud. Consumer prices rose 3.7% over twelve months in September, with a seasonally adjusted 0.6% gain from the prior month — hotter than consensus had positioned for.
The immediate reaction was a flurry of wagers on an October rate hike, according to Reuters. Those bets cooled quickly. By Thursday, investors were largely pricing a hold at the upcoming meeting, while still expecting another increase in December. The distinction matters for bullion: the relief rally reflects a repricing of the near-term decision, not a wholesale shift in the rate trajectory.
That leaves the October 27–28 Fed gathering as the next real test. What policymakers signal about the path ahead will carry more weight than any single data point.
Producer prices add to the pressure
Inflation's grip isn't loosening at the factory gate either. US producer prices climbed 1.3% month-on-month in September and 6.3% year-on-year, yet gold still managed a 1.7% gain on the day. The divergence is instructive — it shows that strong inflation prints don't mechanically translate into weaker gold. On Thursday, the pull of lower yields and a flight to safety simply outweighed the inflation drag.
Bloomberg pointed to a technology selloff tied to concerns over artificial intelligence-related debt as one factor feeding safe-haven demand. UBS strategist Giovanni Staunovo sees a near-term test of USD 4,000 an ounce as plausible, with buyers expected to step in at that level. Over the medium term, the bank looks for higher prices.
China's buying spree has a strategic edge
Underpinning the market is a buyer that doesn't flinch at rate hikes. China imported more than 1,000 tonnes of gold in the first eight months of this year, according to Junge Welt — already surpassing the 886 tonnes it brought in during all of last year. The accumulation has a geopolitical dimension: it forms part of a broader diversification away from the US dollar, a shift that gained urgency after Russian overseas assets were frozen.
The official sector is doing its part. China's central bank added 20 tonnes in August and another 23 tonnes in September, Junge Welt reported, lifting its disclosed reserves above 2,300 tonnes. The build-out extends beyond purchases: Beijing opened a gold storage facility in Hong Kong last year and is weighing additional sites in Singapore, Kuala Lumpur, Dubai and Riyadh — a clear signal that this is a long-term project.
Meanwhile, China's holdings of US Treasuries stood at USD 618 billion in July, the lowest in 18 years, per the US Treasury Department. The decline fits the diversification narrative, though it doesn't by itself prove that those funds are being rotated directly into gold.
ETF flows alone don't set the price
September offered a reminder that demand doesn't guarantee gains. Global gold ETFs took in 67 tonnes during the month, according to the World Gold Council, yet prices still fell. The council cited rising US yields, a firmer dollar and sharply reduced COMEX positioning as the counterweights. Its Tuesday weekly note flagged softening ETF inflows and mixed positioning.
Central banks remain the steadier support. Reported net official-sector purchases reached 39 tonnes in August, bringing the January–August total to 170 tonnes.
That official demand provides a cushion against monetary-policy headwinds — but it doesn't remove them. Thursday's bounce is best read as a recalibration of short-term rate expectations. A more durable recovery would require the twin pressures of a strong dollar and elevated yields to genuinely ease. Until then, gold's path runs through Washington, not through Beijing.

articles.title: Fed set to make interest rate decision as inflation hits 3-year high - ABC7 Los Angeles
articles.summary: Fed set to make interest rate decision as inflation hits 3-year high  ABC7 Los Angeles
articles.full_text:
Futures markets overwhelmingly expect the Fed to hold interest rates steady.
The Federal Reserve is set to announce its latest decision on interest rates on Wednesday as the central bank weathers the highest inflation in three years.
The announcement will mark the first possible adjustment of the benchmark interest rate since Trump nominee Kevin Warsh began his four-year term as Fed chair last month.
The policy move is also set to arrive at a moment of flux for the nation's economy, just days after an agreement between the United States and Iran offered hope for some price relief.
The U.S.-Iran accord, set to be formally signed on Friday, came as gasoline prices fell below $4 a gallon for the first time since March. Still, fuel costs stand well above pre-war levels, and an array of grocery prices remain elevated.
Futures markets overwhelmingly expect the Fed to hold interest rates steady when policymakers meet on Wednesday, according to the CME FedWatch Tool, a measure of investor sentiment.
In recent weeks, however, odds have risen for a potential interest rate hike by the end of 2026, the tool showed, granting a roughly four in 10 chance of a quarter-point increase in December.
The shift in expectations came after a stronger-than-expected jobs report earlier this month showed robust hiring in May. In theory, a resilient labor market could afford central bankers leeway to raise interest rates in an effort to dial back inflation, since elevated borrowing costs risk a hiring slowdown.
Inflation jumped for a third consecutive month as the Iran war continued to drive up prices in May, surpassing 4% for the first time in three years
The Middle East conflict prompted the Iranian closure of the Strait of Hormuz, a maritime trading route that facilitates the transport of about one-fifth of global oil supply. The standoff triggered one of the largest oil shocks ever recorded, sending gasoline prices surging.
On Monday, President Donald Trump announced a U.S.-Iran deal that included plans to reopen the strait. Iranian Deputy Foreign Minister Kazem Gharibabadi confirmed the deal had been finalized and said it would be signed in Switzerland on Friday. Oil prices fell to their lowest level since March.
The benchmark rate stands at a level between 3.5% and 3.75%. That figure marks a significant drop from a recent peak attained in 2023, but borrowing costs remain well above a 0% rate established at the outset of the COVID-19 pandemic.
The rate decision will be the first major policy move overseen by Warsh, who will address reporters during a customary press conference minutes after the central bank issues its announcement.
During his term as a Fed governor in the late 2000s and early 2010s, Warsh gained a reputation as an interest-rate "hawk," meaning he generally preferred higher interest rates as a means of ensuring low and stable inflation.
Last year, Warsh voiced support for lower interest rates. At his Senate confirmation hearing in April, Warsh emphasized the threat posed by elevated inflation.
"When inflation surges -- as it has done in recent years -- grievous harm is done to our citizens, especially to the least well-off," Warsh said.
Bucking typical norms, former Fed Chair Jerome Powell Powell will cast a vote on interest rates as a member of the Fed's 12-person policymaking board.
Powell said he would stay on at the central bank's board of governors after his term as chair expired as an investigation into the Fed's office renovation continues.
The Department of Justice moved to drop a criminal probe into Powell in April, calling on the Fed's inspector general to carry out the investigation into cost overruns tied to the renovation. Powell will remain on the Fed's board for an indeterminate length of time, he said last month.
The criminal investigation into Powell focused on alleged false testimony to Congress about an office renovation. Powell, who was appointed by Trump in 2017, has rebuked the probe as a politically motivated effort to influence interest-rate policy. Trump denied any involvement in the criminal investigation.

articles.title: World Economy Avoids Recession for Now, But Downside Risks Dominate Global Growth Outlook - Goodreturns
articles.summary: World Economy Avoids Recession for Now, But Downside Risks Dominate Global Growth Outlook  Goodreturns
articles.full_text:
The global economy has absorbed the shock of a ten-week closure of the Strait of Hormuz with surprising, if uneven, resilience. But make no mistake - the IMF's April 2026 Global Financial Stability Report is not a comfort letter to investors. It is a carefully documented warning that the architecture of global finance is running warmer than it should, and that the margin for error is vanishing.
Global financial stability risks are elevated, the IMF states bluntly in its latest report. The world is contending simultaneously with the ongoing war in the Middle East, inflationary pressures from an oil supply shock, rising sovereign bond yields, and a cluster of amplification channels - leveraged hedge funds, overstretched private credit, and a derivatives ecosystem that suppresses volatility in calm times only to detonate it during stress. Against this backdrop, every major multilateral institution has revised its growth forecasts, and Wall Street's top banks have been recalibrating recession probabilities almost weekly.
India is the standout in this otherwise subdued landscape. The IMF's April 2026 projections see India growing at 6.2% this year and accelerating to 6.5% in 2027 - a trajectory that makes it the fastest-growing major economy on earth by a significant margin. Domestic consumption, a capital expenditure cycle that predates the current turmoil, and a relatively contained energy import bill compared to Europe are all contributing. India's distance from the direct theatres of conflict - geographically and financially - is proving to be a structural advantage that bond and equity markets are increasingly pricing in.
China, by contrast, is grinding through a slower growth phase. The IMF sees 4.0% in 2026, easing to 3.8% in 2027. Policy support is present but not unlimited, and the technology sector reorientation underway adds medium-term uncertainty to what is already a property-sector hangover. The United States, meanwhile, is on track for 1.8% growth in 2026, with Goldman Sachs recently cutting its 12-month recession probability to 25% from 30% - a modest improvement that chief economist Jan Hatzius attributed to resilient activity data and financial conditions that have eased back below pre-war levels.
Europe is where the stress is most visible in the growth data. The euro area is projected to eke out just 0.9% growth in 2026 before recovering marginally to 1.2% in 2027. Germany, historically the engine of European growth, is in particular difficulty - its energy-intensive industrial base never fully recovered from the post-2022 gas shock, and the Hormuz disruption has created a second consecutive energy cost crisis in three years. The United Kingdom sits in a similar zone of modest growth, with stagflationary pressures - slowing output, persistent services inflation - complicating the Bank of England's already difficult calibration task. Japan, grappling with a historic surge in 40-year Japanese Government Bond yields that hit a record 4.21% in January, is projected to grow just 0.4% in 2026. The Bank of Japan remains the largest domestic holder of JGBs at 51% of outstanding stock - providing a buffer against a disorderly rout - but that concentration itself is a medium-term vulnerability.
The IMF's own Growth-at-Risk framework - which models the full distribution of future growth outcomes rather than just the central forecast - is instructive here. Under prevailing global financial conditions, there is a 5% probability that one-year-ahead global growth falls below 0.75%. That tail risk is at an elevated level historically. But the more alarming detail is in the asymmetry: the upside scenario, where the Hormuz reopens cleanly and energy prices normalise, delivers a Growth-at-Risk improvement to 2.6%. The downside scenario - conditions tighten a further 1.1 standard deviations - pushes the tail GDP outcome to negative 0.5%. The downside is deeper than the upside is tall.
The amplification mechanisms that worry policymakers most are not the headline macro numbers. They are the structural features of modern financial markets that can turn an orderly correction into a cascade. Hedge fund leverage in fixed-income markets has more than doubled since 2020, now exceeding $18 trillion in gross notional exposure. Leveraged exchange-traded funds, which mechanically sell into declining markets at end-of-day rebalancing, have grown rapidly in Asia and the United States. And equity options trading - now running at close to 80% of cash equity volumes - has created a dynamic where zero-day-to-expiry contracts can flip dealer gamma regimes within seconds, turning a modest sell-off into a self-reinforcing rout. None of these mechanisms has detonated yet. But their existence means that if the Hormuz baseline unravels, the velocity of the market response could be far sharper than the underlying economic deterioration would justify.
For India and its investors, the near-term picture is genuinely more benign than the global average. India is a net oil importer, and elevated crude does squeeze the current account. But the rupee, while under pressure, has not experienced the kind of disorderly depreciation that the IMF flags as a specific risk for commodity-importing emerging markets. The Reserve Bank of India's reserve adequacy - above the IMF's metric threshold - gives it meaningful policy headroom that many frontier market peers simply do not have. And crucially, India's financial system is not deeply entangled with the leveraged hedge fund structures or private credit semi-liquid funds that the IMF has identified as the live wires of global financial fragility.
The world, then, is not in recession - yet. But the IMF, the World Bank, and every major Wall Street bank are telling the same story: the base case holds, the tail risk is severe, and the distribution of outcomes is decidedly not symmetric. For investors watching global macro from India, that is not cause for panic. It is cause for precision.

articles.title: Central Bankers Urge 'Collaboration' as AI Reshapes Inflation, Jobs and Financial Stability - Nation Thailand
articles.summary: Central Bankers Urge 'Collaboration' as AI Reshapes Inflation, Jobs and Financial Stability  Nation Thailand
articles.full_text:
G30 panel in Bangkok calls for stronger model testing, classic financial safeguards and early anti-fraud design as AI raises systemic risks.
Stronger testing of AI models, traditional financial safeguards, built-in anti-fraud controls, and tighter cooperation between governments and developers formed the core demands of four of the world’s top policymakers in Bangkok on Saturday (October 17).
Speaking at the Group of Thirty (G30) 41st Annual International Banking Seminar—hosted by the Bank of Thailand as part of the 2026 IMF and World Bank Annual Meetings—Bank of England Governor Andrew Bailey, Central Bank of Nigeria Governor Olayemi Cardoso, IMF Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva, and Bank of Korea Governor Hyun Song Shin agreed that AI is already reshaping global finance and that the window to establish effective guardrails is closing rapidly.
The panel was moderated by Pablo Hernández de Cos, General Manager of the Bank for International Settlements (BIS).
The panel reached clear agreement across five key priorities:
• Rigorous Model Testing: Bailey stated that the foundation for oversight is "stronger model testing standards", applied both before and after commercial release as models continuously evolve.
He noted that evaluating open-weight models presents greater challenges than testing frontier systems such as Anthropic's Mythos, pointing to the UK's AI Safety Institute as a model for public-private collaboration.
• Classic Safeguards: Shin argued that traditional financial tools—capital requirements, leverage limits, collateral, and straightforward rules—remain the most effective defence against market panic, preventing financial firms from becoming simultaneous forced sellers.
• Embedded Anti-Fraud Controls: Bailey urged that new payment infrastructure and tokenised deposits must have fraud protection engineered into their architecture from inception rather than "bolting things on later." 
Cardoso echoed the sentiment, stressing the need to act early "so that the horse doesn't bolt away".
• Arming the Defence: "These models arm the offence. We've got to arm the defence as well," Bailey warned.
• Direct Developer Engagement: Georgieva observed that creating a centralised "world cybersecurity organisation" would be too slow, given that private-sector innovation outpaces bureaucratic frameworks.
While AI developers must have a seat at the table, she stressed that governments should demand total transparency rather than passively accepting industry self-regulation.
She called on the IMF, the Financial Stability Board (FSB), and the BIS to present joint recommendations by the upcoming spring meetings.
When asked for a final takeaway, both Bailey and Cardoso offered a single word: collaboration.
Bailey, who also chairs the FSB, noted that general-purpose technologies have historically expanded economic potential and that AI combined with robotics could drive the next productivity leap.
However, he cautioned policymakers to distinguish between demand and supply effects in both scale and timing. Demand effects, he noted, are arriving first through asset markets, particularly in the United States.
He outlined four primary vulnerabilities that could disrupt stability:
1. Market Corrections: Sudden price drops if investors reassess AI's short-term productivity gains.
2. Lagged Benefits: Slower-than-anticipated returns, echoing past technological revolutions that took decades to show up in macroeconomic data.
3. Corporate Churn: High failure rates among highly valued AI firms ("remember Netscape").
4. Fragile Public Trust: The risk that debt-funded valuations collapse if public confidence wanes.
On broader financial stability, Bailey warned that frontier AI has elevated cyber risk to the top of policy concerns. He revealed that the FSB and UK authorities first grasped the scale of the threat in April, adding that Anthropic's Mythos model "is old technology now."
He also highlighted legal ambiguities, noting that while AI can act as an "economic agent", it cannot be held legally responsible for its actions.
Georgieva argued that AI is currently exerting an inflationary pressure on the global economy through a positive demand shock.
AI-related goods now account for over 10 per cent of international trade, while rising stock valuations create a wealth effect that boosts consumer spending alongside existing pressures from energy, food, and defence costs.
Looking further ahead, she noted that economists remain divided: one camp expects ongoing price pressures driven by energy demand and wealth effects, while another foresees deflation as automation slashes operational costs.
The IMF has not taken a definitive stance.
"We have many more questions than we have answers," she cautioned, advising delegates, "Do not fall for the guys that pretend they have the answers."
She also drew attention to the neglected issue of fiscal and monetary coordination, questioning how tax bases will adapt as labour structures shift.
US data suggests net employment remains positive, but structural shifts are widening income gaps between highly paid, AI-augmented workers and lower-paid service roles as routine jobs contract.
Georgieva identified three major financial stability threats: an abrupt pull-back in AI investment that triggers a broader downturn while the economy is "standing on one leg"; cyber risks "on steroids"; and catastrophic events involving autonomous, rogue AI agents.
Describing her own perspective, she remarked: "Love it, hate it, fear it, it's here." Responding to a question regarding AI entities creating their own financial products, she warned, "If we do not work on guardrails now, we may wake up to something that is not guardrailable anymore."
She compared the required global mobilisation to the preparations for Y2K, warning that current efforts fall well short of that benchmark.
Cardoso emphasised that AI presents emerging economies with a choice between economic convergence or widening divergence, urging developing nations to formulate explicit AI strategies.
His primary concern centers on employment: with roughly 60 per cent of Africa's population under the age of 25, more workers will enter the African job market by 2035 than in the rest of the world combined.
AI that enhances productivity without creating jobs, he warned, poses severe socio-economic risks. He added that central bank credibility will increasingly hinge on data integrity, requiring localised economic models.
On the positive side, AI could accelerate monetary policy transmission in developing nations with underdeveloped banking channels.
Recalling foreign-exchange pressures on the Nigerian naira three years ago driven by virtual assets, Cardoso stressed that technical solutions cannot replace sound fundamentals: "Emerging markets must put their macroeconomic house in order."
Shin described AI's internal mechanics as a "black box" but noted that finance has long managed opaque risks, framing the future as "humans plus AI versus other humans plus AI".
While market participants may use diverse AI models, Shin warned that financial incentives can override algorithmic diversity. During market stress, leveraged institutions are forced to sell simultaneously regardless of their underlying models.
He compared this herd behaviour to London’s Millennium Bridge, which swayed on opening day because pedestrians unconsciously synchronised their steps in response to the structure's movement.
"In finance, the price is the bridge," he noted.
Turning to international payments, Shin described cross-border transfers as "the land that time forgot" due to severe friction and network fragmentation.
To address this, the Bank of Korea is testing "B-Int'l Wire"—an international extension of its large-value payment system that enables foreign banks to hold won accounts and settle transactions directly in central bank money.
Scheduled to launch in January, Shin stressed that success depends less on underlying technology than on regulatory modernisation.
Concluding the session, Hernández de Cos previewed an upcoming BIS survey of households across more than 20 countries, which reveals that while people are optimistic about AI's potential to boost growth, anxiety over job security remains high—particularly among younger and less-educated demographics.
Addressing audience questions on wholesale digital currencies and stablecoins, Bailey highlighted the BIS-led Project Agorá as one of the most promising initiatives for cross-border settlement, while reiterating that private stablecoins must meet the same strict regulatory standards as commercial bank deposits if they are to function as genuine money.

JAKARTA - The surge in energy prices due to the Iran war has prompted a number of major central banks to raise interest rates to curb inflation. However, this move carries other risks. Economic growth could weaken further, even some developed countries could potentially experience a recession by 2027.
According to Anadolu Agency, quoted on Saturday, October 17, the United States Central Bank (The Fed), the European Central Bank (ECB), and the Bank of Japan (BoJ) raised interest rates in September 2026. Meanwhile, the Bank of England (BoE) maintained its interest rate, despite the continued increase in inflationary pressures.
Huw Dixon, professor emeritus of economics at Cardiff University, warned that the energy crisis due to the Iran war had changed inflation forecasts and the direction of monetary policy since the beginning of the year.
He assessed that economic growth could potentially stall by 2027. A recession is also likely in a number of G7 member countries, a group of seven countries with advanced economies.
"Interest rates have to be raised to control inflation. However, we may see interest rates remain high, but below the inflation rate, to limit their impact on the real economy," said Dixon.
The rise in energy prices has left central banks facing a difficult choice. Interest rates need to be raised to hold down inflation, but the cost of borrowing is also hitting households and businesses.
Dixon estimates that central banks will not return to implementing interest rates close to zero as during the 2008 financial crisis, unless there is a conflict with Russia.
US Inflation Soars, The Fed Raises Interest Rates
In the United States, annual inflation rose to 3.7 percent in September, from 3.4 percent in August, according to the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics.
On a monthly basis, consumer prices rose 0.6 percent. A 9.1 percent jump in gasoline prices accounted for more than half of the increase.
Overall energy prices jumped 20.4 percent compared to a year earlier. Gasoline prices rose 34.2 percent, while heating oil soared 74.2 percent.
Core inflation, which does not include food and energy prices, also rose to 2.6 percent from 2.4 percent. Price increases also occurred in housing costs, education, used vehicles, recreation, and air tickets.
The Fed then raised its benchmark rate by 0.25 percentage point to 3.75-4 percent on September 16. The decision was unanimous.
The US central bank judged that inflation was still high so that a rate hike was needed to help bring it back to the 2 percent target.
However, the Fed still sees the economy as quite strong, supported by domestic spending, productivity growth, and investment.
European Inflation Rises, Britain Begins to Feel the Pressure
In the eurozone, annual inflation is expected to rise to 3.8 percent in September, from 3.2 percent in August, according to Eurostat's initial estimate.
Energy inflation rose to 18.8 percent from 14.3 percent. Inflation in the services sector also increased to 3.2 percent from 3 percent.
The ECB raised its three main interest rates by 0.25 percentage points each on September 10. The deposit facility rate, which is the interest paid to banks for funds deposited at the ECB, rose to 2.5 percent.
The ECB warned that the Middle East conflict could keep inflation above target for a long time.
The central bank estimates that average inflation will reach 3 percent in 2026, then fall to 2.5 percent in 2027 and 2.1 percent in 2028.
However, the ECB still projects the eurozone economy to grow 0.9 percent in 2026 and 1.4 percent in 2027. These estimates differ from Dixon's warning about the possibility of a recession.
The ECB sees higher-than-expected inflation risks, while economic growth is potentially weakening. However, the central bank has not confirmed the direction of the next interest rate.
In the UK, the BoE kept its benchmark rate at 3.75 percent on September 17. Six committee members supported the decision, while the other three wanted a rise to 4 percent.
UK inflation was recorded at 3.1 percent in August. The BoE expects the figure to reach 3.75 percent in the fourth quarter and slightly exceed 4 percent by early 2027.
Dixon said before the US and Israeli attacks on Iran, UK inflation was originally expected to fall to 2 percent in April. Interest rates are also expected to fall to a range of 3-3.5 percent.
Now, he estimates inflation will reach 4 percent by the end of 2026 and potentially rise further in 2027 if the war continues.
"The Bank of England's interest rate will go up," he said.
Although the BoE survey showed that the interest rate forecast lasted for quite some time, the movement of the financial market led to a possible increase. The BoE reminded that market prices are also influenced by risk premiums, which are additional yields that investors ask for to face uncertainty.
The increase in borrowing costs is beginning to be felt by the British public. The interest rate on fixed-rate home loans for two years was recorded at around 0.95 percentage points higher than before the conflict.
Japan Raises Interest Rates Despite Inflation Below 2 Percent
Japan is taking similar steps even though its inflation is lower than that of the United States and Europe.
Japanese annual inflation was recorded at 1.9 percent in August. Meanwhile, inflation excluding fresh food prices reached 1.7 percent.
However, the BoJ still raised its short-term interest rate target to around 1.25 percent on September 18. The decision was supported by seven board members, while the other two opposed it.
The BoJ sees its medium- to long-term inflation forecasts continuing to rise. The central bank is also concerned that wage and raw material cost increases that companies pass on to selling prices will push inflation above its 2 percent target.
The high price of crude oil, the weakening of the yen, and the increasing demand for artificial intelligence (AI) related products also add to the price pressure.
The BoJ expects inflation excluding fresh food to exceed 2 percent in the second half of fiscal 2026. The next rate hike is still open, depending on economic and inflation developments.
Dixon warned prolonged uncertainty could undermine confidence in the central bank's ability to maintain price stability.
"Inflation expectations over the past few years have been relatively contained. However, the current uncertainty is so great that this condition could change if central banks again let inflation get out of control," he said.

- Fed Chair Kevin Warsh said he does not “prejudge meetings.”
- U.S. producer prices rose 6.3% annually in September, exceeding the 5.5% forecast

Hello, this is Hui Jie writing from Singapore, filling in for Leonie Kidd. Welcome to another edition of CNBC's Daily Open.
Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh offered markets few clues in his final public appearance before the central bank's October meeting. The latest inflation data, however, may have spoken for him.
Meanwhile, the AI trade had a rough Thursday as investors shifted their attention from what the technology can do to who will pay for it.
CoreWeave, whose debt is showing signs of distress, has become the sector's latest cautionary tale.
In his last public appearance before the Federal Reserve's October meeting, chairman Kevin Warsh gave no signals about where the central bank could go, saying he does not "prejudge meetings." 
"I don't believe in saying now what I might do at the meetings that we have in the balance of this year," Warsh said.
Speaking to the International Monetary Fund's managing director, Kristalina Georgieva, in Bangkok on Friday, Warsh said he observed a "synchronous tightening in monetary policy in most places around the world," which meant there were no "free riders" in the global fight against price increases.
But economic data may provide a clue. U.S. producer prices rose 6.3% in September from a year earlier, hotter than the 5.5% forecast.
Earlier this week, consumer inflation also ran above expectations for September, rising to 3.7% from a year earlier, compared with a 3.6% forecast
AI stocks retreated on Thursday as investor worries over funding mounted, with so-called "neocloud" company CoreWeave front and center in the sell-off.
The company is facing mounting credit stress, with the yield to maturity on its 9.75% bond due in 2031 reaching 15.78%. Yields generally rise when investors view a bond as riskier.
Meanwhile, the spread on its five-year credit default swaps, contracts used to hedge against default, at one point soared above 1,140 basis points.
A spread level of 1,000 basis points or above is generally a sign of credit distress, said Gavan Nolan, executive director of fixed income pricing at S&P Global Market Intelligence.
Investors rotated out of parts of the AI trade amid mounting funding concerns, with Nvidia losing 1.84%, while AMD sank 1.5% and Intel lost about 2.8%. Dell Technologies sank 6.8%.
Collectively, 20 of the most valuable global AI and semiconductor stocks have shed more than $1 trillion in value so far this week, with higher interest rates, concerns about AI financing and intensifying competition weighing on sentiment.
Russia's finance minister attended a Group of 20 meeting in Bangkok on Thursday, marking his second in-person appearance at the event since the 2022 invasion of Ukraine.
Anton Siluanov and Bank of Russia Deputy Governor Elizaveta Danilova were listed as Russia's delegates at the finance ministers' and central bank governors' meetings on the sidelines of the IMF-World Bank Annual Meetings in Bangkok, Thailand, according to a seating plan seen by CNBC.
Siluanov was in the meeting, according to a person familiar with the matter.
The meeting also included German Finance Minister Lars Klingbeil, who had refused to take part a group photo with Siluanov at the August G20 finance ministers' meeting in the U.S. The photo was ultimately taken without the Russian delegation after European officials protested.
Klingbeil reportedly said after Thursday's meeting that "there will be no pretending that Russia is now returning as a normal member of the G20 and simply taking its seat at the table again — not with me, and not with the other Europeans."
— Lim Hui Jie

Hybe's third-quarter revenue is expected to reach 1.5 trillion won ($1.11 billion), up 106% from a year earlier, while operating profit is projected at 172.2 billion won, according to local brokerage firm iM Securities.
Concert revenue is expected to come in at 717 billion won, nearly tripling from a year earlier.

WTI Oil is a type of Crude Oil sold on international markets. The WTI stands for West Texas Intermediate, one of three major types including Brent and Dubai Crude. WTI is also referred to as “light” and “sweet” because of its relatively low gravity and sulfur content respectively. It is considered a high quality Oil that is easily refined. It is sourced in the United States and distributed via the Cushing hub, which is considered “The Pipeline Crossroads of the World”. It is a benchmark for the Oil market and WTI price is frequently quoted in the media.
Like all assets, supply and demand are the key drivers of WTI Oil price. As such, global growth can be a driver of increased demand and vice versa for weak global growth. Political instability, wars, and sanctions can disrupt supply and impact prices. The decisions of OPEC, a group of major Oil-producing countries, is another key driver of price. The value of the US Dollar influences the price of WTI Crude Oil, since Oil is predominantly traded in US Dollars, thus a weaker US Dollar can make Oil more affordable and vice versa.
The weekly Oil inventory reports published by the American Petroleum Institute (API) and the Energy Information Agency (EIA) impact the price of WTI Oil. Changes in inventories reflect fluctuating supply and demand. If the data shows a drop in inventories it can indicate increased demand, pushing up Oil price. Higher inventories can reflect increased supply, pushing down prices. API’s report is published every Tuesday and EIA’s the day after. Their results are usually similar, falling within 1% of each other 75% of the time. The EIA data is considered more reliable, since it is a government agency.
OPEC (Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries) is a group of 12 Oil-producing nations who collectively decide production quotas for member countries at twice-yearly meetings. Their decisions often impact WTI Oil prices. When OPEC decides to lower quotas, it can tighten supply, pushing up Oil prices. When OPEC increases production, it has the opposite effect. articles.summary: Lagarde calls for fiscal discipline as energy inflation strains Europe  finchannel
articles.full_text:
The FINANCIAL — Christine Lagarde called for fiscal discipline on Saturday, Oct. 17, urging governments to keep energy relief temporary and focused on those who need it as Europe confronts renewed inflation and higher borrowing costs. The European Central Bank president said heavily indebted countries should restore room in their budgets through consolidation, revised spending priorities and more efficient public finances.
In her statement to the International Monetary and Financial Committee, Lagarde argued for a measured monetary response to an energy shock too large to ignore. She also said higher long-term interest rates would slow growth and limit the transmission of energy costs into other prices more than the ECB had projected in September.
The statement did not announce a new interest-rate decision. It set out the bank’s assessment of an economy facing pressure on prices alongside tighter financing conditions, with governments also being asked to preserve room to respond to future shocks.
Inflation rises across the euro area
The immediate inflation figures show the scale of the renewed pressure. Euro-area consumer prices were 3.8 percent higher in September than a year earlier, up from a 3.2 percent annual increase in August, according to Eurostat’s October 16 release. Prices increased 0.6 percent from August to September.
Energy prices rose 18.9 percent over the year, compared with 14.3 percent in August. Services inflation increased to 3.2 percent from 3 percent. The measure excluding energy, food, alcohol and tobacco rose to 2.5 percent from 2.4 percent.
The regional average conceals national differences. Annual inflation was 3.3 percent in Germany, 3.4 percent in France, 4.2 percent in Italy and 5 percent in Spain. A year earlier, euro-area inflation had been 2.2 percent. These are European harmonized consumer-price measures, covering a different geography from the United States’ consumer price index.
The ECB’s September rate increase
The ECB’s most recent policy action cited in Lagarde’s statement was a quarter-point increase in September. Its September 10 decision raised all three key rates by 25 basis points, taking effect on September 16. The deposit rate became 2.5 percent, the main refinancing rate 2.65 percent and the marginal lending rate 2.9 percent.
The decision retained the bank’s 2 percent medium-term inflation target and a meeting-by-meeting approach to policy. The ECB said it was not committing itself to a particular path for rates. Its assessment combines the inflation outlook and associated risks, underlying price dynamics and the transmission of monetary policy through the economy.
The bank also continued to let its asset-purchase portfolios decline by not reinvesting principal from maturing securities. It retained its Transmission Protection Instrument, which can address unwarranted, disorderly market movements that seriously threaten the transmission of monetary policy across euro-area countries.
Growth forecasts depend on a fading energy shock
The September ECB staff projections envisaged euro-area growth of 0.9 percent in 2026, 1.4 percent in 2027 and 1.5 percent in 2028. Those figures are forecasts, rather than completed annual growth results. The estimates for 2026 and 2027 had been raised by 0.1 and 0.2 percentage points, respectively, from the June projections.
Staff expected domestic demand to benefit from recovering real incomes and a resilient labor market as energy inflation eased. Infrastructure and defense spending, especially in Germany, and investment related to artificial intelligence were also expected to support activity over the projection period.
The export outlook was more qualified. Strengthening foreign demand was expected to help, but competitiveness problems would continue to constrain exports. The euro area was also expected to benefit less than some other economies from global AI demand because its AI goods sector is smaller.
Irish multinational activity adds another complication to the regional figures. A measure adjusting for that volatility put projected growth at 1.2 percent in both 2026 and 2027, followed by 1.4 percent in 2028.
The cost of protecting households
The International Monetary Fund’s October World Economic Outlook describes a global economy still expanding but facing an uneven recovery. It projects growth of 3.1 percent in 2026 and 3.4 percent in 2027, with global headline inflation at 4.7 percent and 4.1 percent, respectively. The estimates use information available through October 1.
Energy-importing economies outside technology supply chains face the most difficult outlook, the fund said. It identified further conflict, renewed trade tensions, fiscal vulnerabilities and a reassessment of AI expectations among the downside risks. Stronger AI investment and productivity gains, or sustained easing of geopolitical and trade tensions, could improve the outlook.
Its research on cost-of-living crises favors temporary, targeted income transfers that preserve price signals. Measures that suppress prices can require three to 22 times as many fiscal resources as targeted, temporary transfers, the report found. That range is a research finding across the episodes examined, rather than a fixed cost ratio for every government program.
Debt service narrows governments’ options
The IMF’s fiscal researchers have separately described the strain from higher sovereign borrowing costs. The average yield on 10-year government bonds across the Group of Seven rose by more than one percentage point between February and September, reaching its highest level in nearly two decades, according to an IMF fiscal-policy article published October 15.
The fund projects global public debt above 100 percent of global gross domestic product by 2030. It expects the effective average interest cost of government financing to rise from 2.3 percent in 2021 to 3.7 percent in 2031.
For the United States, the article projects interest payments increasing from about 2.8 percent of GDP before the pandemic to 5.7 percent in 2031. Those are projected future payments, rather than a statement of today’s federal interest bill.
Refinancing at shorter maturities can transmit higher policy rates to government budgets more quickly. The researchers also put the global primary deficit at about 3.3 percent of GDP in 2026, compared with roughly 2.6 percent needed to stabilize the debt ratio that year.
Financial markets retain vulnerabilities
The IMF’s October Global Financial Stability Report finds that markets have remained resilient, supported by growth and corporate earnings, while financial risks remain elevated. It identifies a possible correction in AI-related assets, a shock to sovereign bond yields and increasingly sophisticated cyber threats among potential triggers for turmoil.
The report describes the global banking system as broadly resilient, while acknowledging pockets of weaker banks. Among nonbank institutions, liquidity mismatches at insurers and pension funds and leverage in private credit could amplify stress.
Hedge funds hold about $13 trillion in assets globally, more than three times their 2013 level, according to the report. They can support liquidity and price discovery in normal markets. During stress, however, leveraged positions, crowded trades and correlated redemptions can force simultaneous asset sales, with losses or funding strains spreading to other institutions.
American technology finance draws scrutiny
The Reserve Bank of Australia’s October Financial Stability Review documents another connection between the AI boom and credit markets. Technology-related companies accounted for nearly 30 percent of U.S. investment-grade corporate bond issuance in the first half of 2026. That is a share of new issuance, rather than of all outstanding corporate debt.
AI firms are increasingly using corporate bonds, private credit, bank loans and asset-backed financing to fund large projects, the RBA said. It described aggregate leverage as contained and balance sheets as generally healthy, with large technology companies often supported by other revenue streams, including advertising and e-commerce.
Risks differ across the industry. Some data-center developers and cloud-infrastructure providers have weaker balance sheets or concentrated customer bases. Guarantees from larger companies and financing through special-purpose vehicles can support construction, while creating contingent exposures and links among developers, lenders and infrastructure investors. The RBA warned that opaque arrangements can make the industry’s financial exposures harder to assess.
Did euro-area prices fall in September?
No. Eurostat reported a 0.6 percent monthly increase and a 3.8 percent annual increase. A slower inflation rate would mean prices rising more slowly, rather than necessarily falling.
