articles.title: ECB’s Lagarde Pushes Digital Euro and Tokenized Settlement at IMF - The Crypto Times
articles.summary: ECB’s Lagarde Pushes Digital Euro and Tokenized Settlement at IMF  The Crypto Times
articles.full_text:
European Central Bank (ECB) President Christine Lagarde used her October 17 statement to the International Monetary and Financial Committee (IMFC) at the IMF’s Annual Meetings to outline two projects at the intersection of central banking and blockchain-based finance: the digital euro and the Eurosystem’s work to settle tokenized assets in central bank money.
The statement did not explicitly mention crypto assets, stablecoins, or Bitcoin. Instead, Lagarde focused on public-sector payment infrastructure, calling for progress on the digital euro’s legislative framework and highlighting Pontes, the Eurosystem’s distributed-ledger technology (DLT) settlement solution.
The Digital Euro, on a Clock
Lagarde reaffirmed that the ECB is “preparing to complement cash with its digital equivalent” — a central bank digital currency (CBDC), or electronic money issued by a central bank. Unlike commercial bank deposits or privately issued stablecoins, a digital euro would represent central bank money.
Her emphasis was on timing. “Adopting the Regulation on the establishment of the digital euro by the end of 2026 is key,” she said, adding that the Eurosystem plans to run a 12-month internal pilot in the second half of 2027. Both milestones appear in the ECB’s official statement.
That legislative deadline is not the ECB’s to set alone. On July 9, 2026, the European Parliament voted 416 to 169, with 22 abstentions, to advance its negotiating position on the digital euro. The vote cleared the way for negotiations with the Council of the European Union and the European Commission. The European Parliament’s announcement records the vote and the next stage of the legislative process.
These negotiations, commonly called trilogue talks, are intended to produce an agreed legal framework. Lagarde’s end-of-2026 target is therefore a call for the institutions to complete the legislative process, not confirmation that the law has already been adopted.
The 2027 pilot would also be an internal test rather than a public launch. The ECB has selected 36 payment service providers for the planned pilot. A decision to issue the digital euro would remain separate from these preparations and dependent on the legislative process.
Tokenization: Central Bank Money on a Blockchain Rail
The second thread is the Eurosystem’s effort to make central bank money available for settling transactions involving tokenized assets. Lagarde said central bank money must evolve with the digital economy and described the Eurosystem as working to bring its “stability and trust” to digital retail payments and tokenized finance.
Tokenization involves representing assets, such as bonds or funds, as digital tokens on a distributed ledger. The technology can support new ways to transfer and settle assets, but the settlement asset matters too. Transactions may ultimately settle using central bank money, tokenized commercial bank deposits, or privately issued stablecoins, depending on the infrastructure and arrangements used.
The ECB’s approach is to make central bank money available for tokenized financial markets, rather than rely exclusively on private settlement assets. In an October 1 speech, ECB Executive Board member Isabel Schnabel made a related case for central bank money on distributed-ledger infrastructure.
Lagarde also highlighted Pontes, the Eurosystem’s DLT solution, which went live on September 21. According to the ECB’s September 21 announcement, Pontes connects DLT-based platforms with the Eurosystem’s existing settlement infrastructure, allowing eligible transactions involving tokenized assets to settle in central bank money.
The ECB has also begun preparatory work to invest a small part of its own funds in tokenized securities. Its initial focus is euro-denominated debt issued by euro-area governments, agencies and supranational institutions, with purchases to be settled in central bank money through Pontes. The initiative is an early step, not evidence that the ECB is moving its entire investment portfolio on-chain.
A longer-term initiative, Appia, is intended to develop a blueprint for a tokenized financial ecosystem in Europe, based on common standards, shared network infrastructure and European governance. Pontes is the settlement infrastructure now in operation; Appia is the broader ecosystem-development initiative. Neither should be confused with the proposed retail digital euro, which is a separate project.
‘Strategic Autonomy’ and the Stablecoin Context
Lagarde tied the payments agenda to “Europe’s strategic autonomy in payments,” arguing that central bank money must evolve for a digital economy while public and private payment solutions continue to coexist. She did not directly link that phrase to stablecoins or foreign payment networks in the October 17 statement.
The wider policy context is relevant, however. In other settings, ECB officials have argued that the growth of privately issued stablecoins could affect bank deposits, payment revenues and Europe’s dependence on non-European payment providers. In July, ECB Executive Board member Piero Cipollone discussed those concerns while making the case for the digital euro.
That context should not be read as a direct response to Lagarde’s latest statement. Her October 17 address focused on the ECB’s payment and settlement plans; the broader debate over stablecoins and European payment sovereignty comes from separate statements and policy discussions.
Stablecoins are also subject to the European Union’s Markets in Crypto-Assets Regulation (MiCA). The framework’s rules for asset-referenced tokens and e-money tokens began applying in June 2024, while the broader MiCA framework for crypto-asset service providers began applying in December 2024. The European Commission’s MiCA overview sets out the regulation’s scope and implementation.
The contrast is therefore between different parts of Europe’s evolving financial infrastructure: a proposed public digital currency for retail payments, a central-bank-money settlement service for wholesale tokenized assets, and a regulated market for privately issued crypto assets. Lagarde’s statement addressed the first two without naming the third.
The Macroeconomic Backdrop
The digital-money discussion formed part of a broader assessment of the euro-area economy. In the October 17 statement, Lagarde described the economy as resilient but exposed to downside growth risks, including uncertainty linked to the conflict in the Middle East and the resulting energy shock.
The ECB’s September staff projections put euro-area economic growth at 0.9% in 2026, 1.4% in 2027, and 1.5% in 2028. The statement also noted that energy prices were expected to keep headline inflation above the ECB’s target into the first half of 2027 before easing.
On monetary policy, Lagarde confirmed that the ECB raised its key interest rates by 25 basis points in June and again in September. She also flagged financial-stability risks associated with geopolitical tensions, private credit markets and the concentration of critical third-party technology providers.
The statement raised concerns about the cybersecurity implications of advanced artificial intelligence models, saying new frontier AI models had increased cyber risks and operational vulnerabilities. These remarks were part of the ECB’s broader financial-stability assessment, rather than a warning directed specifically at crypto markets.
Why It Matters
For digital-asset markets, Lagarde’s statement illustrates how Europe’s central bank is advancing its own approach to digital money and tokenized financial infrastructure. The digital euro remains dependent on legislation, with an internal pilot planned for the second half of 2027. Pontes, meanwhile, is live as a settlement service intended to connect eligible tokenized-asset transactions with central bank money.
The key distinction is between the ECB’s stated plans and the wider implications for private digital assets. The statement supports the conclusion that the Eurosystem is developing public infrastructure for digital payments and tokenized finance. It does not, by itself, establish that the ECB intends to displace stablecoins or that private settlement assets will not play a role in European markets.
The projects also remain at different stages. The digital euro has not been issued, and its enabling legislation is still under negotiation. Pontes has entered operation, but the ECB’s planned tokenized-securities investments are limited in scope, while Appia remains focused on developing a longer-term blueprint.
How public and private settlement options will coexist as tokenized finance develops remains an open question. The ECB’s statement sets out its direction of travel, but does not settle that debate.

Investing.com -- Chinese artificial intelligence supply-chain companies are expected to continue pursuing Hong Kong listings despite growing valuation concerns and increased investor scrutiny, according to Citigroup.
Simon Yuan, Citi's head of China investment banking, said demand for Chinese AI-related listings remains resilient despite recent valuation pullbacks affecting data centre companies, particularly in the U.S.
Speaking on the sidelines of the International Monetary Fund's annual meetings in Bangkok, Yuan said Hong Kong's IPO market benefits from a relatively balanced mix of domestic Chinese and international investors.
Growing southbound investment flows from mainland China have also strengthened the market's liquidity, providing support for companies seeking to raise capital.
However, Yuan warned that Hong Kong would not be immune to a broader correction in global AI valuations.
He said a significant downturn in the U.S. AI investment cycle could affect markets worldwide, including Hong Kong, following increased volatility in recent weeks.
Chinese hardware manufacturers have benefited from rising global demand for AI infrastructure, recording higher sales volumes alongside stronger unit prices.
Many companies have also established manufacturing operations outside mainland China, allowing them to serve international customers while reducing exposure to geopolitical tensions.
Looking ahead, Yuan expects Hong Kong's equity capital markets to shift their focus next year from AI hardware suppliers towards Chinese AI model developers and application companies.
However, he cautioned that prospective issuers would need to demonstrate sustainable business models, strong revenue growth and profitability to attract investors.
The outlook comes amid a strong year for Hong Kong's IPO market, supported by Chinese technology companies seeking fresh capital.
A total of 118 companies were listed in Hong Kong during the first nine months of 2026, raising HK 388 billion (49.4 billion), representing a 106% increase from the corresponding period last year.
The figures highlight continued investor appetite for Chinese technology listings, even as concerns over elevated AI valuations create uncertainty across global equity markets.

articles.title: Gold could hit record highs by 2028 as central banks ramp up buying: Report - The Financial Express

articles.full_text:
Gold prices could reach fresh record highs within the next two years as central banks increase bullion purchases and investors seek protection against geopolitical tensions, rising government debt and economic uncertainty, reports businesstoday.in citing the Financial Times.
The report said fund managers expect gold prices to rise over the medium to long term, supported by demand for safe-haven assets and concerns about government finances and currency stability. Central-bank purchases have also emerged as an important driver of the precious metal's outlook.
Gold prices rose 2% to $4,075 per troy ounce on Wednesday, as investors assessed expectations that the US Federal Reserve could raise interest rates again, the Financial Times reported.
Central-bank buying supports gold outlook
Provisional data from the World Gold Council cited in the report showed that central banks purchased around 63 tonnes of gold in September, the highest monthly level since November 2024. The figures were compiled using central-bank and International Monetary Fund data.
Gold crossed $5,500 per ounce once in January following a sharp rally, although prices subsequently retreated. The metal has nevertheless remained at historically elevated levels.
The outlook comes as gold and silver prices recover some ground in international markets after a sharp selloff earlier in the week. On Friday, October 16, COMEX gold futures were trading at $4,177.50 per ounce, up 0.18%, while silver futures gained 0.48% to $57.43 per ounce.
Domestic bullion prices, however, remained under pressure. Gold prices in New Delhi fell by ₹900 to ₹1.49 lakh per 10 grams on Thursday, marking a fourth consecutive session of declines. Silver prices dropped ₹6,000 to ₹2.15 lakh per kilogram, according to PTI. A stronger rupee and subdued physical demand weighed on domestic prices.
Government debt and geopolitical risks drive demand
Speaking at the Financial Times' Precious Metals Symposium, Charlotte Yonge, a fund manager at Troy Asset Management, said gold could provide a hedge against deteriorating government finances. She pointed to rising US government debt and the possibility of central banks expanding money supply if the global economy enters a recession.
Paul Carne, delegated chief investment officer for Europe, the Middle East and Africa at Aon Investments, also expected gold to reach new records within two years. He suggested that weakening confidence in the US dollar could encourage investors to turn towards gold.
Peter Marrone, chair and chief executive of Allied Gold, said investors should consider whether their portfolios were prepared for a potential financial crisis. He added that deteriorating economic conditions could prompt investors to shift some holdings away from government bonds towards gold.
Ian Cockerill, chief executive of Endeavour Mining, highlighted concerns about currency depreciation and said central banks were increasingly focused on protecting the value of their reserves.
Interest-rate outlook remains a key risk
Near-term price movements will also depend on US inflation and Federal Reserve policy expectations. September US consumer inflation rose 3.7%, above the expected 3.6%, raising concerns that interest rates could remain elevated for longer.
Higher interest rates and bond yields tend to weigh on gold and silver because the metals do not generate interest income. A stronger dollar can also make bullion more expensive for buyers using other currencies.
Geopolitical tensions in West Asia could support safe-haven demand, but their impact may be offset by movements in the dollar and bond yields. In India, currency movements, import costs and domestic demand will also influence prices.
Despite the near-term risks, continued central-bank purchases and investor demand for protection against economic uncertainty could support gold over the coming two years, the Financial Times report suggested, according to businesstoday.in.

articles.title: The dress rehearsal for an AI reckoning - Financial Times
articles.summary: The dress rehearsal for an AI reckoning  Financial TimesThe AI bubble is about to burst — and a big market correction is coming  New York PostWall St Week Ahead As AI rally wobbles, stock market's spotlight turns to earnings  ReutersThe Global AI Bust: What Will Survive When the Boom Ends  Foreign AffairsAI Bubble: It's Not One Bubble, But Three Ready To Burst (SPX)  Seeking Alpha
articles.full_text:
Roula Khalaf, Editor of the FT, selects her favourite stories in this weekly newsletter.
The past week brought a lively and very useful dress rehearsal for what a bursting of the AI bubble in markets might look like.
First off, we got a hint of what will probably cause it: not cold hard economics, not a blown fuse in an arcane bit of financial wiring, but vibes. That was what really did the damage this week.
Every investor on the planet knows the problems here. We have a highly concentrated global stock market that is trundling along almost entirely on the fumes of speculative excitement about this one big theme. We have eye-watering levels of borrowing, often laced with rather creative ways to shove leverage off balance sheets and into places where rating agencies and investors find it hard to spot. The supposed finest minds in the industry blame “agents” and “worms” when their technology causes havoc, and still no one knows whether it can all make enough money to pay the bills when they fall due.
We all know this. And we know global financial markets, and all our pensions and savings nestled inside them, are vulnerable if anything goes wrong. Surveys of professional investors now place AI exuberance and the hyperscaler debt binge at the top of worry lists. Just to hammer the point home, it takes some effort to avoid hearing the constant warnings from central banks and bodies such as the IMF and the Bank for International Settlements that we must not assume this will go on forever and we must be ready for systemic shocks when the music stops.
All of this was true months ago just as much as in the second half of this week — nothing had really changed. But the trade wobbled significantly nonetheless. South Korea’s famously chip-heavy stock market sank 8 per cent in a day. Bonds issued by pure-play data centre companies took a beating and, ominously, credit default swaps — a kind of derivative that acts as protection against debt defaults — on some issuers rocketed higher. A reasonable rule of thumb in markets is that whenever you hear the letters C, D and S in one sentence, something bad is happening.
It was not a full-on market reversal — conspicuously, the US still managed to hold up on the day. But the second big lesson was a taste of what a true AI shock might do to financial markets.
We saw two sure signs that investors were truly spooked: nice, boring, non-techy stocks such as those in the UK’s FTSE 100 outperformed. Also, US government bonds, heavily bruised after a run of beatings, finally picked up — a sign that investors want safe assets, and that they think an AI implosion could scupper the miracle that is US economic growth. Data earlier in the week showed US inflation is simply not backing down — a dynamic that would usually punish debt markets — but bonds still picked up handily, pulling benchmark 10-year yields back down towards 5 per cent.
Unusually, given this bout of nerves, the dollar weakened pretty significantly — the DXY dollar index is down almost 1 per cent since the middle of the week — lending weight to the theory that the piercing of the AI bubble would lead to a global retreat from US markets and dollar assets.
So this is the outline of what end times might look like: a weaker dollar, stronger bonds, a hammering for markets hooked on the semiconductor boom and a preference for old-economy stocks. Good to know.
But determining when to reach for those safety plays is harder because traders and investors cannot pick out one solid event that rumbled markets this week. They point to several things: the alarm ringing from inside the house, in the form of Broadcom’s chief executive warning that chips investors are treating markets like a “casino”; the breezy ambition of CoreWeave to tap insurers for funding because “that’s all the money in the world”; and the failure of efforts to list data centre companies on stock markets in Australia and Asia.
None of these things matter so much in isolation. But put them all together and you have a growing pool of evidence that the brightest days of the AI trade are behind us. The easy money has been made, and now investors are asking tougher questions.
That vague sense that “something could go wrong” is starting to really gnaw at investors, as George Saravelos at Deutsche Bank observed in a recent note. Systemic risks could stem from “a safety event, a failed [stock market listing], or disappointing revenues”, he said. “Concentration risk is immense, and it is this . . . event risk that is most underpriced in markets at the moment.”
The good news for investors who struggle to shake the feeling that we are overdue a big pullback in the runaway AI trade is that the classic safe retreat — developed-market government debt — is deep in the bargain basement. Even after this week’s sizeable pick-up in bond prices, long-term yields are still around their highest level in decades. It is not clever or fancy, but sticking to tried and tested bets such as this does stand out among the options.
The trickier task is figuring out where the next wobble might come from and what might flip it from a stumble to a crash. The AI trade has lived by the vibes, and it will die by the vibes.

articles.summary: Stocks Have Ignored 5% Treasury Yields — JPMorgan Strategist Says AI May Be Changing The Rules  Stocktwits
articles.full_text:
Stocks have continued to hold up even as Treasury yields surge to levels that historically would have raised serious concerns for equities, prompting JPMorgan to question whether the market’s relationship with interest rates has fundamentally changed.
The 10-year Treasury yield briefly touched 5.36% earlier this week, its highest level since 2002, after rising 112 basis points since the end of 2025. The move has investors asking a familiar question: At what point do higher yields finally become a problem for stocks?
Historically, there was a relatively clear relationship between Treasury yields and stocks, according to JPMorgan Asset Management’s Chief Market Strategist for the Americas, Gabriela Santos.
When yields were low and rising because of stronger economic growth, stocks generally benefited alongside them. But once yields crossed a certain threshold, the relationship flipped, with higher rates beginning to weigh on equities.
“Intuitively that makes a lot of sense,” Santos wrote.
She identified two distinct historical thresholds. From 1965 through late 2008, stocks and yields generally moved together until the 10-year Treasury reached about 4.5%.
From 2009 through mid-2021, that threshold fell to roughly 3.5%, reflecting a weaker-growth, lower-inflation environment.
But the post-2021 period looks very different. “The new new normal?” Santos asked.
Since mid-2021, the relationship between Treasury yields and stocks has become far less predictable, with correlations repeatedly moving between positive and negative. In other words, there may no longer be a single yield level that automatically signals trouble for equities, she noted.
The iShares 20+ Year Treasury Bond ETF (TLT) fell 0.02% in Friday’s after-hours session, while the iShares 7-10 Year Treasury Bond ETF (IEF) was flat.
Santos believes part of the explanation lies in how dramatically the composition of the stock market has changed.
The 10 largest companies now account for roughly 40% of the S&P 500, according to Santos, and many of those companies are being driven less by traditional economic activity and more by the artificial intelligence investment boom.
That could help explain why stocks have remained resilient despite the sharp increase in borrowing costs.
While major technology companies have begun issuing debt to fund massive AI infrastructure spending, Santos does not believe higher rates at current levels are necessarily enough to derail their growth trajectory.
“The looser relationship between yields and stocks is also likely due to the changing nature of the market and its dominant earnings driver,” Santos wrote.
For now, the strategist says investors may need to watch something other than the 10-year yield itself.
“Bond yields and stocks may continue to beat to the sound of their own drum,” Santos wrote, with the most important drivers being “the AI capex boom, the ability of the hyperscalers to monetize that investment, and ultimately the adoption of that technology across sectors.”
That means the old question of how high can Treasury yields go before stocks break may no longer have the simple answer investors once expected, she added.
During the after-hours session on Friday, the SPDR S&P 500 ETF (SPY), which tracks the S&P 500 index, was flat; the Invesco QQQ Trust ETF (QQQ) edged up by 0.01%; and the SPDR Dow Jones Industrial Average ETF Trust (DIA) rose 0.02%. Retail sentiment on Stocktwits toward the S&P 500 ETF was in the ‘bullish’ territory at the time of writing.

The weather story that helped fuel grain-market optimism is beginning to unravel. Improving rainfall across the U.S. Plains, favorable early-season conditions in South America, and substantial speculative exposure could leave corn, soybeans, and wheat vulnerable to additional selling.
Part of the big summer rally in grains was due to inflationary fears of higher crude oil prices and multiple wars. Of course, some of it was weather, but still the US just produced a record soybean crop and the second largest corn crop ever.
So much for all of this “bull” - painting death and destruction to US grain crops. It was the wheat crop, which was affected the most last spring. In fact, US wheat production was the lowest in 73 years. That is already built into wheat prices.
The important distinction is that a bearish weather outlook does not automatically mean a permanent end to the grain bull market. It means the burden of proof is shifting back to the bulls.
I caught the top of the wheat market weeks ago, and I felt that the Ukraine-Russia war was built into prices and that the easing Plains drought would create a swarm of bullish traders running for the hills.

My early call on the Plains wheat drought
Weeks ago, my longer-range analysis anticipated that the stubborn drought across the US Plains wheat belt would begin easing.
Rather than extrapolating summer drought indefinitely, my ClimatePredict approach emphasized changing global atmospheric circulation patterns, including the developing strong El Niño, and the potential for more favorable autumn rainfall.
That distinction matters enormously to wheat traders.
Wheat prices often build in a weather-risk premium when producers are planting into dry soils. However, once widespread rainfall begins replenishing soil moisture, the market may start discounting better establishment of the winter wheat crop months before harvest.
My forecast was not simply about rain arriving on a particular day. It was about recognizing a broader seasonal shift that could reduce the threat to winter wheat production.
The lesson for commodity traders: Sometimes the most profitable weather forecast is identifying when a drought-driven bullish narrative is about to lose its credibility.
The biggest danger: Funds are still heavily long corn and soybeans
This is particularly important because large speculative net-long positions represent potential future selling pressure. If favorable South American weather persists and USDA production remains large, fund managers may be forced to reduce exposure even without a major new bearish surprise.
The October USDA report was particularly damaging to corn’s bullish narrative. USDA estimated US corn production at approximately 16.034 billion bushels, surprising traders who had expected a reduction in production.
There are, nevertheless, two reasons not to become excessively bearish.
First, the recent very wet Midwest weather could still cause harvest delays, quality problems, and localized yield losses. Second, USDA’s October production estimate is not necessarily its final word. There remains some possibility of downward adjustments in subsequent reports.
South America: Why the next 60–90 days matter
For now, the favorable South American weather scenario is bearish for grain prices, particularly soybeans.
- Brazil soybeans: Favorable planting moisture and timely rains would encourage acreage establishment and strong early growth.
- Argentina corn and soybeans: Adequate moisture during planting and early development would reduce concerns about immediate crop stress.
- El Niño uncertainty: A strong El Niño can increase the likelihood of wetter conditions in portions of southern Brazil and Argentina, but rainfall distribution matters. Excessive rainfall, flooding, or later heat and dryness could still alter production expectations.
These are conditional weather assessments, rather than verified statements that every major growing region currently has ideal soil moisture.
For soybeans especially, the market will need to consider whether strong Brazilian production prospects could eventually outweigh supportive US crush demand and relatively tight domestic supplies.

The Dow is headed for a weekly gain of 1%, and it rose as high as 52,539.36 just before 10 a.m., up 361.67 points, before giving back part of that move.
Volatility is easing even as the Nasdaq slips. The CBOE Volatility Index is at 15.88, down 3.51% and below Thursday’s 16.46. Wednesday’s spike to 16.87 came with a 1.1% drop in the S&P 500 and a 1.9% drop in the Nasdaq. Two days later, fear gauges are lower and the tech-heavy index is down again. Traders are not hedging a crash. They are moving money out of one group and into another.
The 10-year Treasury yield is steady at 5.09% after falling 10 basis points on Thursday. The 30-year yield is at 5.43%. With long rates at those levels, any company that funds growth with debt is being valued like a credit instrument, and that is driving everything else in this market.
Thursday’s rebound set up the morning. The Dow gained 556.21 points to 52,177.69. The S&P 500 added 25.12 points to 7,744.06 and the Nasdaq added 20.16 points to 26,713.03. Volume reached 20.7 billion shares against a 20-session average of 17.6 billion, and advancers beat decliners 3.1-to-1 on the S&P 500. Friday is repeating that pattern of wide participation, but with tech weighing on the headline numbers.
Day Structure: Firm Futures, a Quiet Warsh, Then a Nasdaq Fade
The session started on a stable footing overnight. Before dawn in New York, S&P 500 futures were at 7,803.75, up 12.75 points, and Dow futures were at 52,616, up 186 points. Nasdaq futures were the weak spot at 30,112.25, down 31.50 points. Russell 2000 futures were up 0.36% at 2,791.70. That split held through every phase of the morning.
The overnight event was Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh’s fireside chat at the IMF–World Bank Annual Meetings in Bangkok. Warsh gave no signal on the October decision. S&P 500 and Nasdaq futures edged higher after his remarks, Asian equity indexes were steady, and Treasury yields barely moved. The market treated a lack of hawkish surprise as good news.
Before the open, broad buying was already visible in stocks that trade before the bell. S&P 500 members that had moved were rising more than 2-to-1, with 224 higher, 106 lower and 173 unchanged. Chip names were the exception and kept falling through the premarket session. The SPDR S&P 500 ETF was quoted at $773.03, up 0.16% from Thursday’s $771.79 close. The Invesco QQQ Trust was down 0.16% and the iShares Russell 2000 ETF was up 0.29%.
Bank and insurance earnings hit before the bell. Truist and Travelers both traded lower, and Citizens, Regions and M&T Bank also reported. Alcoa traded higher on its after-hours report from Thursday. Tesla rose as much as 5.4% before the bell after unveiling its Roadster. CoreWeave fell 5% before the open, erasing much of Thursday’s late surge.
At the 9:30 a.m. bell, the Dow was up 0.4%, the S&P 500 up 0.1% and the Nasdaq down 0.3%. The S&P 500’s first print was 7,745.32, and it reached its session high of 7,756.84 within minutes.
Then the bid faded in the largest names. By 9:54 a.m. the S&P 500 had slipped to 7,742.25 while the Dow climbed to 52,539.36 and the Nasdaq dropped to 26,530.57. By 10:10 a.m. the Nasdaq loss had grown to 0.79% and the S&P 500 had turned negative at 7,735.22.
Most stocks did not follow the indexes down. At the turn of the hour, close to four in five S&P 500 stocks were rising, with advancers ahead 4-to-1. Ten of 11 sectors were green, led by financials and energy. The cap-weighted index is falling because its biggest technology weights are falling, not because the average stock is weak.
Friday also has a moderate data load. September import and export prices and September industrial production are scheduled, with consensus forecasts of 0.8% for imports, 1% for exports and 0.4% for production. The September federal budget balance has a consensus deficit of $34.70 billion, against a $167 billion deficit in August. None of these releases has yet moved the trade enough to change its direction.
Chips on the Edge of a Nine-Session Losing Streak
The weakest group in the market is semiconductors, and the losses are wide. The iShares Semiconductor ETF (SOXX) is down more than 2% this morning and is heading for a ninth straight decline. That would be its longest losing streak since May 2006. After that 2006 streak ended, the fund fell another 17% before bottoming in July. This sector has seen this setup before.
SOXX closed Thursday at $514.71, down 0.91%. Its five-session loss through Thursday was 8.62%. It is still up 68.80% year to date, with a 52-week range of $260.44 to $655.95. Thursday’s trading ran from $495.79 to $517.12 on 16.44 million shares, double its 8.16 million average. Heavy volume on down days means investors are selling, not just stepping back.
Within a 60-stock semiconductor basket, 57 names are down this morning. That kind of near-total selling is what an asset-allocation shift looks like, not a reaction to one company’s news.
Micron is the biggest single drag. The memory maker is at $895.82, down $35.42 or 3.80%, with its market value back to $1.014 trillion. Its 52-week range runs from $192.40 to $1,255.00, so it is now 29% below its peak while still up 360% over 12 months. Micron was quoted at $912.80 before the bell and has lost more ground since the open.
SK hynix ADRs are down 5.34% to $138.31. Intel is down 2.77% to $92.73, valuing the company at $490.2 billion, with 17.8 million shares traded in the first 40 minutes. Super Micro Computer has dropped 5.33% to $33.22. Sandisk was quoted at $1,362 before the open, down 2.35%.
Nvidia is holding up better than the rest of the group. It is at $216.36, down 0.40%, with a market capitalization of $5.224 trillion. It fell 1.84% on Thursday to $217.23. Nvidia funds its own expansion from operating cash. The names falling hardest are the ones whose customers, or the companies themselves, rely on bond markets to build capacity.
That split is the clearest reading of this week. AI hardware is not being sold as one group. The market is separating firms that self-fund from firms that depend on financing, and in a market with a 5.09% 10-year yield the second group is being treated as rate-sensitive. Thursday’s chip losses were cut short by a 10-basis-point drop in yields. Friday’s yields are flat, and the chips are falling again.
Upside catalysts exist, but they come later. Big Tech earnings start next week, and those reports will show whether the capital spending that drives chip demand is being maintained or cut.
CoreWeave CRWV and the AI Credit Trade
CoreWeave is the stock most directly tied to the AI financing worries this week, and it is falling again. Shares are at $64.11, down $5.58 or 8.01%, on 20.4 million shares by 10:12 a.m. Its market capitalization is $35.36 billion. The 52-week range of $59.51 to $141.79 shows how much has been lost: the stock is 55% below its high and down 49% over 12 months.
Thursday was a big reversal. CoreWeave traded between $59.51 and $69.76, dipping below $60 to touch its late-July lows before closing at $69.69, up 5.94%. Friday’s drop has erased most of that rebound. The $60 level is now the key support. If it holds, Thursday’s break below it was a false breakdown. If it fails, the rebound was only a short squeeze. Overhead, the $70 strike, which carries large options open interest, and the $92 to $93 area are the next resistance points.
The credit markets are driving the stock. CoreWeave’s five-year credit default swap spread rose 16% to a record 1.14% before easing to 1.03%. Its 2031 bonds yield 15.78%. The company has more than $50 billion in debt. Since October 6, the spread on that default protection has widened sharply, and that rise lines up closely with the share price slide.
A bond yielding 15.78% from a company at the center of AI infrastructure tells investors exactly how lenders view the risk. When the 10-year Treasury pays 5.09%, a spread above 10 percentage points prices in real default risk, not just the cost of funding a fast-growing company. Equity investors are following the lead of bond holders.
Nvidia, CoreWeave’s second-largest shareholder with a 10% stake, tried to calm the market. articles.full_text:
US Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh said in Bangkok on Friday that the global economy has proved surprisingly resilient and called AI the most consequential change of his lifetime, but gave no hint on interest rates ahead of the Fed’s meeting this month.
The global economy has held up better than Kevin Warsh would have predicted earlier this year, the US central bank chief said on Friday, calling AI the biggest economic shift he had seen.
Speaking in Bangkok at the annual meetings of the IMF and the World Bank, Warsh offered no clue on the Federal Reserve’s next rate decision, due on 28 October.
Almost everywhere, the economy is showing a resilience "I’m not sure I would have predicted five or six months ago," Warsh said in a discussion on stage with IMF chief Kristalina Georgieva.
The Fed chair was most upbeat about the US, stating during the event that a broadening investment surge that "isn’t just AI" had given the economy "plenty of tailwinds", momentum "certainly not found everywhere in the world".
Energy prices have soared since the US and Israel went to war with Iran in late February. This, along with an AI investment boom, has fuelled inflation in many economies, forcing central banks to raise rates.
The Fed, which has seen inflation run above its 2% target for over five years, raised rates by a quarter point to 3.75-4% in September, its first hike since July 2023.
"At the Federal Reserve, we made very clear that we would deliver price stability," argued Warsh, who took over as chair in May.
He said he had heard the same "resolve" from central bankers in Bangkok, calling the wave of rate hikes, including two by the European Central Bank, a "synchronous tightening" that leaves "no free riders".
The IMF on Tuesday nudged up its 2026 global growth forecast to 3.1% but said risks were tilted to the downside. Rich countries also face soaring borrowing costs, with the 10-year US bond yield above 5% and the French bond yield trading around 4.8% at the time of writing.
A 'bumpy' road for AI
Much of Friday's discussion focused on AI, which Warsh said was "probably the most consequential change" for the US and global economies in his lifetime.
Before taking office, he had argued that an AI-driven productivity boom could curb inflation and make room for lower interest rates. On Friday, he acknowledged that for now, the investment frenzy was pushing prices up by fuelling demand.
Minutes of the Fed's September meeting noted that data centre construction had driven up the cost of chips, computer equipment and electrical components.
However, over time, Warsh expects AI to boost the economy’s capacity to produce, bringing a "huge benefit" at home and abroad.
He also expects it to change central banking as "we torture data with old-fashioned models," he said. "Not so long from now, it won’t be torture."
Despite the optimism, the Fed chair also warned that the road ahead was "likely to be a very bumpy one", both in understanding the technology and because "we really don’t know what the market structure is going to be".
Eyes on the next Federal Reserve meeting
Warsh, who has promised fewer hints about where policy is heading, kept to that pledge.
"I don’t prejudge meetings," he said, though he noted the world had "broadly conformed" to the Fed’s expectations since September.
US consumer price inflation rose to 3.7% in September from 3.4% as petrol prices surged, though core inflation, which excludes food and energy, was 2.6%.
Wholesale prices rose 6.3% year on year, the most since 2022, while the economy added just 29,000 jobs last month.
Bets on an October hike have swung this week, jumping from about 22% to around 50% after Wednesday’s inflation figures before falling back to about 30%, according to CME FedWatch, a tool that tracks market pricing.
Markets currently put the chance of a December hike at around 90%, while the September minutes showed that most Fed officials expect another hike this year.
New York Fed President John Williams, vice chair of the Fed’s committee, told Bloomberg on Tuesday that "it may be appropriate to have one more rate hike", but saw no need for more in 2027.
On the other hand, Fed Governor Michelle Bowman said at the Bangkok meetings on Wednesday that she felt no urgency to act.
The decision comes days before the 3 November US midterm elections.
September’s hike defied US President Donald Trump’s demands for lower rates, though he still backs Warsh, his pick for the job.
Friday’s remarks were among Warsh’s last before the Fed’s quiet period, which starts on Saturday and bars officials from discussing policy until after the meeting. Investors will next hear from him at his press conference after the decision.

(Kitco News) – Gold prices staged a late-week recovery after coming under heavy pressure from hotter-than-expected U.S. inflation data, rising Treasury yields, and a firmer dollar, as falling bond yields and reduced expectations for an October Federal Reserve rate hike helped the precious metal recover much of its losses.
Spot gold kicked off the week trading at $4,193.59 per ounce on Sunday evening, and the yellow metal briefly climbed above $4,200 as traders continued to monitor the U.S.-Iran conflict and inflation risks from elevated energy prices. The advance quickly faded, however, with gold setting its weekly high at $4,216.91 per ounce on Monday before a stronger dollar and rising Treasury yields pushed prices lower through Tuesday’s trading session.
The selling accelerated Wednesday after September CPI rose 3.7% annually, exceeding expectations and reinforcing concerns that energy-driven inflation could force the Fed to tighten monetary policy again. Gold broke below $4,100 and set its weekly low at $4,073.35 per ounce at noon on Wednesday, as traders increased bets on an October rate hike and the dollar strengthened.
Gold rebounded Thursday despite another hotter-than-expected inflation reading from the Producer Price Index, as Treasury yields retreated sharply from recent highs while the dollar weakened. The recovery carried into Friday after Fed Chair Kevin Warsh on Thursday evening refrained from signaling an October rate increase, helping reduce immediate tightening expectations even as markets continued to anticipate another hike before year-end. Gold briefly approached $4,200 once again before stopping short and surrendering some of its gains to trade marginally lower on the week and the session heading into the weekend.
The latest Kitco News Weekly Gold Survey showed half of Wall Street on the fence on gold’s near-term price direction, while less than half of Main Street sentiment creeped closer to a bearish majority after another failed breakout.
“I am neutral on gold for the coming week,” said Colin Cieszynski, chief market strategist at SIA Wealth Management. “Gold appears to be hanging around the $4,200 level at the moment and there is less economic data due next week to move it as focus turns to corporate earnings.”
“Up,” said Darin Newsom, senior market analyst at Barchart.com. “I don’t care about technical (Dec gold is in an intermediate-term uptrend on its weekly chart) or fundamental (central banks around the world continue to buy gold) analysis at this point. Given this, long-term investors might get interested in gold again if everything else is destroyed over the weekend. I’ll spend this weekend watching the 1964 classic ‘Dr. Strangelove’ and listening to R.E.M.’s ‘It’s the End of the World as We Know It.’”
“Unchanged,” said Adrian Day, president of Adrian Day Asset Management. “I remain in the camp that sees some more back and forth before gold breaks out. It is coming soon, however. Gold’s resilience in the face of a run-up in yields, and relatively strong dollar and oil prices, is telling. Gold is well supported on the downside, so it’s now a matter of time before it breaks out. But an end to the war – which would bring with it a lower dollar and lower oil price leading to reduced inflation and rate hike expectations – is the likely catalyst.”
“Up,” said James Stanley, senior market strategist at Forex.com. “Strong late-week response, and while there’s still a case for continued digestion as price is building in a falling wedge pattern, I still want to bias this as ‘up’ until I have reason not to. The $4k level in spot remains the major level of note, and until there’s a convincing breach of that, I’m probably going to remain bullish.”
Fawad Razaqzada, market analyst at StoneX Bullion, said that despite gold’s midweek rebound, he remains doubtful prices have seen a bottom.
“Yes, the US dollar has eased a bit and the reversal in Treasury yields are also helping,” he said. “But while the immediate pressure has eased, I would be reluctant to interpret [Thursday’s] gains as a clear signal that the correction is over. For now, at least, my near-term gold outlook remains modestly bearish, even if I have a strong long-term bullish bias towards gold and especially silver.”
Razaqzada said he is waiting for confirmation that gold has formed a low. “The metal has tried to hold key support around $4,100, but the resistance zone overhead has held firm,” he said. “I would need to see a move above that zone before turning bullish at current levels. Thus, the technical gold outlook still hangs in the balance.”
“Up,” said Rich Checkan, president and COO of Asset Strategies International. “With the U.S. dollar weakening for the first time in five weeks, gold should benefit. Buyers of gold in currencies other than the U.S. dollar will find their gold ultimately cheaper with the more favorable exchange rate.”
Naeem Aslam, chief investment officer at Zaye Capital Markets, believes gold’s outlook will depend on whether persistent inflation outweighs the pressure from potentially elevated interest rates.
“Thursday’s retreat in Treasury yields and the dollar provided support for bullion despite stronger wholesale inflation, demonstrating that gold responds to changing real-yield expectations rather than inflation figures alone,” he said. “Analysts should monitor the $4,154 price area as near-term support and $4,179 as immediate resistance, alongside Treasury yields, dollar strength, central bank guidance and developments affecting global energy supplies. A sustained decline in real yields could encourage additional institutional diversification into gold, while renewed monetary tightening expectations may trigger consolidation. We therefore see inflation uncertainty, geopolitical hedging and shifting monetary policy expectations as the principal forces shaping gold’s price direction through the remainder of 2026.”
“Lower,” said Adam Button, head of currency strategy at investingLive. “I struggle to see how the Fed only hikes by the 70 bps that's now priced into the curve. This week's inflation data was a big problem that's being overlooked because of the worries about AI debt.”
Daniel Pavilonis, senior commodities broker at StoneX Group, told Kitco News that gold remains an inverse 10-year Treasury yield play, with the rise and fall of the yield determining whether investors should be long or short the precious metal.
“We're seeing something similar to what we saw in the seventies, with high interest rates and sticky inflation,” he said. “Certain sectors of the markets or the economy do well... and other ones don't. Right now, it seems like AI is pretty strong with the infrastructure buildouts. But maybe there's some truth to [the idea] that it's not just the energy sector that's driving inflation, but also this demand structure from the AI boom, and instead of money going into buying U.S. Treasuries or something like that, they're spending the money on AI infrastructure.”
Pavilonis said the limited inverse response of yields and gold to this week’s inflation data was interesting.
“We had CPI out, we had PPI out, and CPI was a big number,” he noted. “Ten-year yields did not break the highs, right? They went up to 5.299%, and the previous high was like 5.32% or something like that. If you're looking at candlesticks on the 10-year yield, and you're looking at candlesticks on the gold market, it literally looks just flipped, identical but flipped.”
“Yesterday, we saw a continuation of a breakdown in yields, and gold seemed to be having a good day.”
Looking ahead, Pavilonis said he’ll be watching these key thresholds in both yields and the gold price for indications of where the precious metal could be headed.
“I think if rates can continue to sell off… maybe the Fed is just going to keep yields higher at the front end of the curve and then the back end just starts to unwind due to the uncertainty in the economy,” he said. “I think that's what's going to drive the metals here.”
“Zooming out and looking at some of these markets, if yields run up to 8% then where does that leave gold? I would say at the very least $3500,” he said. “Same thing with silver, where would silver be? I would say maybe below $40. So that's really what we're looking at here.”
Pavilonis said many of the things that were driving gold and silver’s price gains at this time last year are not there anymore.
“The headlines, the market drivers, interest rates were lower… this was all pre-Iran,” he said. “Now we have the Iran situation, and it's causing inflation, but the metals are not that big of an inflation hedge. articles.full_text:
The gold investment boom in India has run into a roadblock. Several mutual fund houses have temporarily stopped accepting fresh lump-sum investments, new systematic investment plans (SIPs) and switch-ins into Gold and Silver ETF Fund-of-Funds from October 16, amid the government's efforts to rein in gold imports and ease pressure on the rupee.
Sources said there was no directive from the regulator to stop flows into gold funds. A source from the Association of Mutual Funds in India (AMFI) also confirmed there had been no discussion about stopping investments in gold funds at the industry level.
"The stoppage is entirely the call of the respective funds. It is not an industry-wide call — in fact, there is no such discussion at the industry level," said a source.
The decisions appear to have been taken independently by the respective asset management companies, potentially in anticipation of increased demand for precious metals during the festive season and the possible implications for the rupee.
The timing is significant. Gold ETFs have emerged as a major channel for investors seeking exposure to the yellow metal, particularly after the Sovereign Gold Bond scheme was discontinued in February 2024. Inflows into Gold ETFs surged from Rs 9,225 crore in 2024 to Rs 42,961 crore in 2025.
The momentum has continued this year. Gold ETFs attracted net inflows of Rs 45,926 crore between January and September 2026, despite outflows in May. January alone saw inflows of Rs 24,040 crore, followed by Rs 5,255 crore in February and Rs 2,266 crore in March. Inflows stood at Rs 3,040 crore in April, before a net outflow of Rs 725 crore in May. The subsequent four months saw inflows of Rs 3,443 crore in June, Rs 1,559 crore in July, Rs 2,597 crore in August and Rs 4,451 crore in September.
The halt comes against the backdrop of an increasingly strong government push to temper India's appetite for gold. Prime Minister Narendra Modi made two appeals this year — in May and again on September 1 — urging citizens to avoid buying gold and gold jewellery for at least a year unless absolutely necessary.
India produces virtually no commercial gold and imports nearly 85-90% of its consumption. The gold import bill hit a record $72 billion in FY26, adding to the country's foreign exchange burden. With the West Asia conflict pushing up crude oil prices, India is facing additional dollar outflows at a time when the government is seeking to curb non-essential imports.
The government has also raised import duties on gold and silver from 6% to 15%. The combined effect of the appeals and higher duties appears to be reflected in import volumes. Between January and September 2026, gold imports declined 6% year-on-year, while silver imports fell 35%.
The latest restrictions on fresh investments in Gold and Silver ETF Fund-of-Funds add another dimension to the effort to moderate demand for precious metals, coming just ahead of major festive buying periods such as Dhanteras and Diwali.
Although ETFs are often described as paper gold, every unit of a Gold ETF is backed by physical gold held in secure, insured bank vaults. Money flowing into these products therefore ultimately represents demand for physical gold, even though investors buy units through the financial market rather than purchasing jewellery or bullion directly.
Prithviraj Kothari, president of the India Bullion and Jewellers Association, described the move as temporary and a step in the right direction to curb the rupee's decline against the dollar.
"The retail will buy physical in smaller quantity versus funds that buy bigger amounts," he said, suggesting that restricting fund flows could help moderate large-scale purchases of gold.
The suspension comes at a time when gold has become a preferred investment avenue for Indian investors, even as pressure on the country's external sector has made curbing gold imports a policy priority.
The restrictions, communicated to investors through addenda, cover fresh lump-sum investments, additional lump-sum investments, switch-ins, top-ups and new SIP registrations. New systematic transfer plan (STP) registrations have also been restricted under the relevant communications.
However, instalments under existing SIPs and STPs registered before the effective date will continue to be processed at the applicable net asset value (NAV). Redemptions, switch-outs and instalments under existing systematic withdrawal plans (SWPs) will also remain permitted, in accordance with the respective scheme documents.
So far, HDFC Mutual Fund, Invesco Mutual Fund, ICICI Prudential Asset Management Company and Tata Mutual Fund have made such announcements.

The MLC, with a low volume of operations, is approximately at 652 pesos, a figure that should be viewed with caution.
The United States dollar (USD)
The United States dollar is trading at 805 Cuban pesos (CUP) at the close of this Saturday. This represents an increase of 2.5 pesos compared to the previous day, when it closed at 803 CUP.
In the last week, the currency has risen by 22.5 pesos —a 2.9% increase— from the 783 CUP it was at seven days ago. Over the past month, the dollar has gained a total of 102.5 pesos compared to the 703 CUP from 30 days ago, although it is important to note that this comparison may partially reflect methodological adjustments in the index.
Exchange Rate Evolution
In the last 30 days, the highest recorded was 805 CUP and the lowest was 703 CUP. It continues to reflect the pulse of the informal market in a context of structural currency shortages.
The euro (EUR)
The euro closes at 904 Cuban pesos (CUP), compared to 898 CUP in the previous session, marking an increase of 6 pesos for the day — a 0.7% rise.
Compared to seven days ago, when it was at 876 CUP, the European currency has increased by 28 pesos, equivalent to 3.2%.
In the last month, the euro has gained 106 pesos from 798 CUP thirty days ago, although this variation may include methodological adjustments of the index.
The maximum of the last 30 days stands at 905 CUP and the minimum at 798 CUP. It surpasses the dollar by 99 pesos, consolidating its dominant position in the Cuban parallel market.
The MLC
The MLC closes with a reference value of 652 Cuban pesos (CUP), with caution due to the low volume of transactions recorded during this time period.
This represents an increase of 20 pesos compared to the previous day, when it was at 632 CUP.

articles.title: Spanish savers seek shelter from inflation as deposit rates stagnate - todoalicante.es
articles.summary: Spanish savers seek shelter from inflation as deposit rates stagnate  todoalicante.es
articles.full_text:
Cristina Cándido
A record level of savings, but a dismal performance on returns. Spanish households have never held as much money in banks and investments as they do today, boasting a net wealth of €2.8 trillion—excluding mortgages and consumer debt. Yet a third of that capital remains idle in current accounts, vulnerable to the erosive impact of inflation. Caught between a rising cost of living, the housing crisis, and a deep-seated attachment to cash, families are steadily migrating towards alternative savings vehicles, with digital challenger banks and high-yield accounts gaining significant traction.
Spanish savers maintain a conservative asset allocation dominated by cash and deposits, which account for 32% of the total, according to the latest Bank of Spain figures up to the second quarter of 2026. Mutual funds follow at some distance, reaching an all-time high of 17.5%, followed by equities (14.3%), and insurance and pension schemes (11.4%). At the other end of the spectrum, fixed income and Treasury bills represent barely 1% of gross wealth, despite their recent rapid surge.
To understand the current climate, one must look back to 2022. Between that summer and the end of 2023, the European Central Bank implemented the fastest interest-rate hike in its history—lifting the deposit facility to 4%—to curb soaring inflation following the outbreak of war in Ukraine. Shielded by an excess of accumulated liquidity, Spain’s major Ibex 35 banks kept current account returns virtually frozen at around 0.1%, passing rate increases onto term deposits at a notably slower pace than their eurozone peers.
This disconnect between surging prices and banking inertia sparked an unprecedented shift starting in early 2023 and continuing throughout 2024 and 2025. Households withdrew billions from their accounts to seek shelter, initially in Spanish Treasury bills (Letras del Tesoro) and later in fixed-income funds. By 2026, amid another bout of inflation triggered by conflict in the Middle East, savers are once again venturing beyond high street bank branches to safeguard their purchasing power. Consequently, money traditionally left languishing in cash and deposits has steadily dwindled, falling to 32% of total household wealth by the end of June 2026, down from 38.6% in 2022.
Cash holdings in Spanish household portfolios have fallen to 32% from 38.6% in 2022, according to Bank of Spain figures
"Spanish savers are, on the whole, overly conservative. Even when they invest, they do so far too cautiously—for instance, in short-term fixed income or Treasury bills, which offer yields that rarely beat inflation and therefore erode purchasing power," warns Josep Soler, founder and executive director of the Spanish financial planning association EFPA. In his view, this defensive posture stems from both limited financial literacy and cultural tendencies to prioritise "a theoretical preservation of capital that fails to materialise in practice", coupled with unwarranted optimism about state pensions maintaining future living standards.
High-yield accounts
Capitalising on these conditions, digital banks and investment platforms have used deposit interest rates as their main Trojan horse to attract customers. In contrast to traditional Spanish high street lenders, which have historically focused on selling mutual funds through their branches to bolster fee income, fintechs such as Revolut, Trade Republic, and N26 are offering no-strings-attached high-yield accounts yielding between 2.5% and nearly 4%, paying interest on a monthly or even daily basis.
The total capital drawn in by these platforms remains modest when compared with the more than €950 billion still sitting in current accounts at major banks. Yet their impact has broken the monopoly of the physical branch network, particularly among younger savers, compelling incumbent lenders to launch cash incentives for salary direct debits in an attempt to stem the outflow of clients.
Challenger banks are offering high-yield accounts with returns ranging from 2.5% to nearly 4%
Combining pure-play digital banks, the online arms of major lenders (such as Openbank or Evo Banco), and direct banking models like ING, challenger platforms now command roughly 10% of the market. The key to their success? "Low fees, above-average yields, a catalogue of products tailored to contemporary demands, and an entirely digital experience," explain analysts at the comparison site HelpMyCash.com.
The ascent of these alternative platforms is underscored by the latest MyInvestor Barometer in October 2026: nearly six in ten respondents (59.7%) identify interest-bearing accounts as their primary vehicle for savings over a twelve-month horizon, making it the preferred stepping stone for those moving capital away from traditional banks for the first time.
Fixed-term deposits
Fixed-term deposits have historically been the default choice for Spanish savers. However, figures reveal a striking departure from historical norms: according to Inverco data up to June 2026, the 'other deposits' category (which encompasses term deposits) stands at just €188.13 billion, representing a modest 5.2% of total household financial assets. Spanish families currently hold five times more wealth in ordinary current accounts (€951.27 billion) than in interest-bearing fixed-term deposits. This stands in stark contrast to previous economic cycles, when term deposits routinely accounted for more than 24% of household financial savings.
With the former network of regional savings banks (cajas) long gone and market concentration high, major lenders have preferred to reserve competitive interest rates for customers willing to commit to heavy cross-selling—such as substantial salary deposits, life insurance, or private pension schemes. Alternatively, they channel liquidity into "hybrid deposits", which require savers to allocate half their capital into fee-generating mutual funds.
In this environment, mid-sized lenders and foreign institutions have disrupted the deposit market. Providers such as Renault Bank, Pibank, Banca March, and EBN Banco, alongside cross-border deposit platforms like Raisin, enable retail savers to access accounts in Italian, Portuguese, or French banks offering rates above 3%, all backed by European deposit guarantee schemes.
Treasury bills
Where major banks refused to open their vaults, the Spanish state stepped directly into households' financial planning. Direct retail holdings of short-term Treasury bills (Letras del Tesoro) experienced unprecedented growth, surging from a negligible €212 million in 2021 to an all-time peak of over €25.9 billion by late 2023, driven by yields nearing 3.8%. Far from evaporating once the European Central Bank began trimming interest rates and the queues outside the Bank of Spain subsided, retail appetite for sovereign debt has become an established digital routine.
At the close of the first half of the year, Spanish households held €19.56 billion in Letras and a further €16.30 billion in government bonds. Savers have not returned these funds to their current accounts; instead, the vast majority have reinvested maturing debt online via the Treasury portal, concluding that lending directly to the government remains a far superior haven compared to leaving cash dormant in bank accounts.
Developments this autumn confirm this pattern, demonstrating that investor appetite for securing yield without credit risk remains entirely resilient. Following a brief dip when expectations of monetary easing drove yields down to around 2.8%, auctions in September and October pushed yields higher once more. In early October, the marginal yield on 12-month bills climbed back above the 3% mark (reaching 3.026%, its highest level since summer 2024), while nine-month paper hovered just beneath 3%.
Mutual funds
Despite the prominence of alternative savings products, the undisputed beneficiary of this capital flight has been the collective investment industry. Fresh data indicates that the search for returns, coupled with geopolitical uncertainty, has driven assets in mutual funds and investment vehicles to an all-time peak of 17.5% of household financial assets.
In the first half of this year alone, Spanish households poured €25.18 billion of fresh capital into mutual funds, taking total assets under management to €639.04 billion—closing in on the €640 billion threshold. Behind this record lies not speculative appetite for equities, but a distinct preference for lower-risk assets, particularly fixed-income funds, which have emerged as one of the favoured destinations for family savings.
This boom reflects a blend of commercial strategy and tax incentives. For the banking sector, fixed-income funds have proven to be an effective vehicle to steer customer savings into products delivering attractive returns without the need to raise deposit rates, all while generating steady fee revenue through management charges.
More than 73% of investors plan to turn to index funds to counter market volatility and inflation, according to MyInvestor
Underpinning this appeal is the favourable tax treatment enjoyed by mutual funds in Spain. Unlike deposit interest or Treasury bill gains—which are taxed upon maturity—funds permit investors to defer capital gains tax when transferring capital between eligible funds without cashing out. This flexibility allows savers to rebalance portfolios according to market conditions without triggering an immediate tax liability on accumulated gains.
Appetite for collective investments is set to remain strong into next year, notably through passive management. According to the MyInvestor Barometer, more than 73% of investors plan to allocate capital to index funds over the next twelve months—a figure exceeding 80% among those under 44—seeking to navigate an environment widely expected to be defined by stock market volatility and persistent inflation.

Global oil prices surged on Friday, with Brent crude climbing above $110 a barrel for the first time since May, as investors assessed the impact of escalating tensions involving Iran and the intensifying Russia-Ukraine war on global energy supplies.
Brent crude futures breached the $110 threshold shortly after 2:30 p.m. Eastern Time, marking a five-month high and intensifying concerns over the potential impact of rising energy costs on consumers, businesses and financial markets.
Meanwhile, US benchmark West Texas Intermediate (WTI) crude rose 3.5% to settle at $101.41 a barrel, moving above the $100 mark for the first time since September. The price level remains a closely watched indicator for traders and consumers as higher crude costs feed into fuel prices.

Fuel Costs Face Further Upward Pressure
The latest surge in oil prices threatens to push US gasoline prices higher in the coming days, adding to the financial pressure on households already facing elevated fuel costs.
The average price of regular gasoline across the United States stood at $4.32 per gallon on Friday morning, reflecting the continued strain on energy markets.
Diesel futures also climbed by more than 1% during Friday’s session. Diesel prices have risen particularly sharply in recent months, outpacing increases in regular gasoline and raising concerns for industries heavily dependent on the fuel, including agriculture, manufacturing and freight transportation.
Higher diesel costs can ripple through supply chains, increasing the expense of transporting goods and operating machinery, potentially adding to inflationary pressures across the wider economy.
Iran Tensions and Russia-Ukraine War Disrupt Supply
The latest rally comes amid mounting concerns over disruptions to global energy flows linked to geopolitical conflicts.
Fuel prices worldwide began rising gradually in the spring following US and Israeli attacks on Iran in late February, which led to the closure of the Strait of Hormuz, a critical maritime corridor for international energy shipments.
Meanwhile, the intensifying Russia-Ukraine war has placed additional pressure on diesel markets. Russia has historically been one of the world's largest diesel exporters, but Ukrainian attacks on Russian energy infrastructure have taken significant refining capacity offline.
Russian strikes have also damaged energy facilities in Ukraine, further complicating regional fuel supply and distribution.
As a result, buyers that previously relied on Russian diesel have been forced to seek alternative sources, adding pressure to an already constrained market.
Refining Capacity Limits Supply Response
The prospect of rapidly increasing diesel production remains limited, as refineries in the United States and Europe are already operating at or near capacity to maximize output.
These constraints could prolong the impact of supply disruptions, particularly if geopolitical tensions continue to affect refining operations and international fuel shipments.
With limited spare refining capacity available, any further disruption could intensify competition for diesel supplies and keep prices elevated.
Rising Energy Prices Weigh on Wall Street
Higher energy costs also contributed to a broader decline in US equities on Friday.
The S&P 500 fell more than 1%, while the Nasdaq dropped approximately 2% by mid-afternoon, as investors weighed the economic implications of rising oil prices.
Sustained increases in energy costs can complicate the outlook for inflation, corporate earnings and consumer spending, adding uncertainty to financial markets.
Trump Faces Pressure Over Fuel Prices Ahead of Midterm Elections
The surge in fuel prices presents a political and economic challenge for President Donald Trump ahead of the US midterm elections scheduled for November 3.
Diesel prices are particularly significant because of their direct influence on transportation, agriculture and industrial activity, making them an important channel through which energy costs can feed into broader inflation.
Trump has reportedly pressed US allies to release some of their diesel and crude oil reserves in an effort to ease supply pressures. He also recently signed a measure relaxing regulatory restrictions on the use of red-dyed diesel, a fuel generally designated for off-road applications.
However, the effectiveness of such measures in offsetting global supply disruptions remains uncertain as geopolitical risks continue to shape energy markets.
Outlook: Energy Markets Remain Vulnerable
The latest price rally underscores the vulnerability of global energy markets to simultaneous disruptions across major producing regions and critical shipping routes.
With Brent crude above $110 a barrel, US oil prices exceeding $100 and diesel supplies constrained by limited refining flexibility, the risk of further fuel-cost increases remains a concern for consumers, businesses and policymakers.

articles.title: US debt interest costs hit $3 billion a day and jumped 8% in 2026—faster than spending, revenue, GDP - Fortune
articles.summary: US debt interest costs hit $3 billion a day and jumped 8% in 2026—faster than spending, revenue, GDP  FortuneThe US federal budget deficit for 2026 just came in. It’s $1.992 trillion.  Yahoo FinanceA $2 trillion deficit looms over the midterms  CNNU.S. budget deficit swells to almost $2 trillion for fiscal 2026, up 12% in a single year  CNBCU.S. Budget Deficit Nears $2 Trillion, a Reality Check for Trump’s Cost Cutting  The New York Times
articles.full_text:
The federal government’s fiscal year ended last month, and the final tally offered another stark warning about the trajectory of U.S. debt.
According to Treasury Department data released on Friday, the federal budget deficit widened to $1.99 trillion, 12% worse than the $1.78 trillion gap in fiscal 2025.
That came as revenue increased 3% to $5.4 trillion, lagging behind the 6% bump in spending to $7.4 trillion. Social Security and Medicare were the biggest line items, but in third place was interest payments on the national debt, topping defense spending and Medicaid.
Gross interest costs for fiscal 2026 came in at $1.36 trillion, Treasury data show, with an average interest rate of 3.53%. That’s more than double the rate in 2021, just before the Federal Reserve embarked on an aggressive tightening cycle to rein in inflation.
Net interest payments rose 8% to $1.05 trillion, outpacing increases in total spending, revenue and GDP. In fact, it exceeds real GDP growth of about 2% as well as nominal GDP growth of about 6%.
Fiscal 2026’s net interest costs translate to about $2.9 billion a day, and the Peter G. Peterson Foundation estimated they represent 3.2% of GDP, breaking the previous record set in 1991.
With gross U.S. debt at $40 trillion, publicly held debt at 100% of GDP, and borrowing costs up, interest payments are projected to be the fastest growing portion of the federal budget in the coming years.
At the same time, the debt burden is being increasingly exposed to market volatility that threatens to make interest costs even steeper.
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has been issuing more short-term debt to finance the deficit and is retiring long-term obligations.
Now, about one-third of publicly held debt, or more than $10 trillion, is due to mature within the next 12 months, meaning the federal government must roll it over at today’s higher rates.
In February, the Congressional Budget Office projected annual debt interest expenses will reach $2.1 trillion by 2036. But then President Donald Trump launched the Iran war, which sent oil prices and bond yields soaring.
The 10-year Treasury yield is now above 5%, blowing past the CBO’s forecasts for 4.1% this year, 4.2% in 2027, 4.3% from 2028 to 2031, and 4.4% from 2032 to 2036.
If bond yields remain about 1 percentage point above the CBO’s estimates, interest costs will surge to $2.8 trillion, or 5.9% of GDP, by the end of the decade, according to the Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget.
“Higher interest begets more debt, and greater debt begets higher rates and higher interest. Eventually, the whole thing could come crashing down,” CRFB President Maya MacGuineas said last month.
“That’s why Washington needs a fiscal intervention now, before it’s too late. The President, the Treasury Secretary, and Congressional leadership need to understand the severity of this issue. There are no easy fixes, and we can’t just wish this problem away.”
But so far, there’s no sign of much willingness to tackle spending or revenue. Trump has even called for a $5,000 “dividend” check to Americans if Republicans win the midterm elections and is already handing out “rebates” to millions of Medicare and Affordable Care Act enrollees.
Meanwhile, Bessent has argued that heating up the economy further can get the debt under control.
“With 3% growth, we grow our way out of this,” he said at Southern Methodist University last month. “We’ll get to the other side of this Iran conflict, and the underlying economy is very, very strong, and I think reaccelerating.”
But CBO Director Phillip Swagel said last week that faster economic growth is unlikely to keep U.S. debt in check. While stronger economic growth will help by bringing in more revenue for the federal government, it’s not that simple.
Federal spending also boosts growth, which lifts wages that in turn affect outlays on Social Security benefits, he pointed out. A robust economy also tends to send interest rates higher, which adds to debt interest costs.
Assuming interest rates of 4% to 5%, Swagel estimated that nominal GDP growth would have to reach 7%-8%, and real GDP growth would have to hit 5%-6% in order to stabilize the debt.
That’s more than double the latest real GDP pace of 2.2% in the second quarter. Meanwhile, even bullish Wall Street forecasts put full-year GDP growth at 2.5%.
“So growth will help, but it’s probably not plausible that growth alone will stabilize our fiscal trajectory,” he said. “So then we’re left with changes in revenues and changes in spending, and those are political choices.”
