Editor’s Note: It’s been an ugly week to own AI stocks. A hotter-than-expected inflation print sent rates jumping, and the most leveraged names in the trade took the worst of it – CoreWeave has now fallen more than 40% since mid-August, and Oracle hasn’t fared much better.
Here’s why I’m handing today’s issue to Jonathan Rose: he called it. Back in August – with CoreWeave trading near $106 – Jonathan went on his live show and named it and Oracle as the two AI stocks most exposed if the market turned. He even titled the episode “AI House of Cards.” And he wasn’t guessing.
After years trading on the Chicago exchange floors, Jonathan watches signals most stock investors never check – like what it costs a company to borrow money. Those signals were flashing in August. The stock market caught up this week. Below, he tells the story of how he spotted it and how you can learn to see the same warnings before the crowd does.
One more thing: Jonathan just released his free $10K to $100K Challenge presentation, where he lays out the full strategy – how he finds unusual trading activity, evaluates the opportunity, and defines his maximum risk before entering any trade. Watch it after you read this; it’ll make even more sense then.
Now, here’s Jonathan.
In October 2015, a natural gas well near Los Angeles started leaking methane.
And I don’t mean a little leak. This thing was a catastrophe.
The leak came from an underground storage facility tucked into the mountains just above LA’s sprawling San Fernando Valley. Soon, a rotten-egg stench was drifting through nearby neighborhoods.
Residents reported headaches, nausea, and nosebleeds. Thousands of families fled to hotels and temporary housing, with no idea when they could return. Two local schools had to be relocated.
The leak wouldn’t be stopped for 111 days.
But something about the coverage bothered me. Every article talked about Southern California Gas Co.
OK. But I had an additional question: Who owned SoCalGas?
The Important Company Wasn’t the One in the Headlines
Turns out the parent company was Sempra (SRE), a publicly traded utility.
I pulled up Sempra on my screener and found something that stopped me cold. Somebody had made an unusually large bearish trade against the company.
I had two pieces of information: a major environmental disaster involving a Sempra subsidiary… and a big bearish trade in the parent company’s stock.
I didn’t know who placed that trade or what they knew. But I’d spent years trading on the floors of the Chicago exchanges, where I learned to pay attention when large trades show up in unusual places.
Somebody was putting real money behind a bet that Sempra was going lower.
So I shared a bearish trade of my own with my followers. With it, we risked $200 for the opportunity to make $4,800.
A few days later, California declared a state of emergency, and Sempra’s stock plunged. One of my followers later told me he’d made $9,600 after risking $400.
Here’s another part I love.
I found a reporter covering the leak who hadn’t mentioned Sempra, so I reached out and pointed out that SoCalGas had a publicly traded parent company. She wrote back that she was working on a follow-up.
That’s what I mean when I talk about following the money.
While everybody was watching the gas leak, I was watching the company behind it – and what traders were doing with its stock.
This August, I spotted something similar in a very different business: artificial intelligence.
Why CoreWeave and Oracle Looked Vulnerable Before the AI Selloff
On August 17, I was hosting my daily Masters in Trading LIVE show. We were talking about retail earnings and consumer health.
Then I changed the subject to two AI companies that had me worried: CoreWeave Inc. (CRWV) and Oracle Corp. (ORCL).
Now, I’m still very bullish on AI. I love what Nvidia Corp. (NVDA) is doing. I think artificial intelligence will create enormous opportunities for years to come.
But that doesn’t make every AI company a good investment.
CoreWeave and Oracle were borrowing enormous amounts of money to build AI infrastructure.
CoreWeave rents computing power to AI companies. That means buying expensive chips, building data centers, and spending a fortune before all that equipment generates revenue.
Oracle is making its own enormous investments in AI data centers, with a substantial portion of its future business tied to OpenAI.
Then there’s what’s called “circular financing.”
Nvidia sells chips to CoreWeave. Nvidia also owns a stake in CoreWeave. AI companies sign massive agreements to rent computing capacity. The companies providing that capacity borrow money to buy more equipment.
Big AI Contracts Don’t Eliminate Financing Risk
Everybody announces another billion-dollar deal, and investors get excited.
But I have a question: Where is all this money actually coming from?
When companies borrow billions and funnel money among the same group of businesses, those impressive deals can conceal a great deal of financial risk.
That’s why I called my August 17 show the AI House of Cards.
I told viewers that if the market turned, CoreWeave and Oracle would be among the first companies to get hit. I didn’t want to be long either stock. In fact, I suggested CoreWeave shareholders consider taking their profits.
CoreWeave was trading around $106 when I issued my warning.
CoreWeave’s Bond Market Flashed the Warning First
Now, I need you guys to stay awake for a minute. I’m going to talk about bonds.
I know, I know. Everybody’s favorite subject.
But this is important.
Most investors watching CoreWeave were looking at the stock price, Nvidia, and all those enormous AI deals. I was looking at what it cost CoreWeave to borrow money.
CoreWeave had issued bonds paying 9.6% interest, but those bonds were now trading at prices that pushed the yield to around 15%. That’s a massive jump.
That means investors were demanding much more compensation to take on CoreWeave’s risk. Somebody was getting nervous. And the warning appeared in the debt market before it became obvious in the stock price.
Oracle was showing warning signs, too. The cost of insuring its debt against default had risen sharply.
When you’re borrowing billions to build data centers, the cost of money matters. And when lenders get nervous, stockholders had better pay attention.
Then the AI Selloff Hit the Most Leveraged Name
On October 15, I revisited CoreWeave and Oracle during Masters in Trading LIVE.
CoreWeave had fallen from approximately $106 on August 17 to around $61. That’s a decline of roughly 42% in less than two months.
Oracle had taken a beating, too. Other AI infrastructure names were under pressure.
The immediate trigger wasn’t necessarily a new discovery about AI. Hotter-than-expected inflation raised concerns about interest rates and borrowing costs.
And companies carrying enormous financial obligations were particularly vulnerable. That’s what worried me in August.
Look, CoreWeave has real customers and an enormous backlog of contracted business. Some investors see a tremendous opportunity after this decline.
Fine.
But there’s a difference between having billions in business lined up and having the financial strength to deliver it profitably. And when you borrow heavily to fund growth, you don’t have much room for things to go wrong.
Here’s another thing I told viewers on Thursday. I wouldn’t make a new bearish trade on CoreWeave at $61.

That’s why I always want to know my risk before entering a trade.

Think back to that natural gas leak in California.
I didn’t predict the disaster. I figured out which publicly traded company was exposed and found unusual trading activity that suggested an opportunity.
With CoreWeave and Oracle, the setup was different. I was looking at financial risks building underneath two popular AI stocks.
But the principle is the same: Don’t just watch the headlines. Follow the money.
That’s the approach behind my premium trading service. We watch for unusual trading activity – large trades that stand out from the normal buying and selling.
Not every big trade means something, and not every trade works out. But when somebody puts serious money behind an unusual position, I want to know about it.

Jio Platforms IPO Attracts Rs 2.5 Lakh Crore in Investor Demand Ahead of Listing
Jio Platforms’ proposed IPO has reportedly attracted nearly Rs 2.5 lakh crore in investor interest, including global asset managers, sovereign wealth funds, Indian mutual funds and insurers.
Jio Platforms’ proposed initial public offering (IPO) has reportedly drawn investor demand worth nearly Rs 2.5 lakh crore, with major global asset managers, sovereign wealth funds and leading Indian financial institutions among those seeking an allocation, according to a report by Moneycontrol citing people familiar with the matter.
The reported interest comes ahead of the offering, which is expected to give investors an opportunity to purchase shares in Jio Platforms as a separately listed entity. The company, a subsidiary of Reliance Industries, operates across telecommunications and a range of digital services.
- Jio Platforms IPO reportedly drew massive Rs 2.5 lakh crore demand.
- Global and Indian financial institutions expressed significant interest.
- Listing allows investment in Jio's diverse digital services portfolio.
Among the investors reported to have expressed interest are the Life Insurance Corporation of India (LIC), SBI Mutual Fund and HDFC Mutual Fund. Global investment firms Fidelity Investments, Capital Group and BlackRock are also among the names cited in the report.
Global Sovereign Funds And Asset Managers Show Interest
The reported demand includes several prominent sovereign wealth funds, including Singapore’s GIC, Norway’s Norges Bank Investment Management, Abu Dhabi Investment Authority (ADIA) and Qatar Investment Authority (QIA).
According to the people cited in the report, interest has also come from foreign long-only funds, India's 10 largest mutual fund houses and its five largest insurance companies.
Beyond conventional institutional investors, technology-focused global investors and large family offices have reportedly indicated sizeable interest in the proposed offering.
The scale and diversity of the reported demand point to interest from investors with different investment strategies and geographical backgrounds. However, the reported demand represents investor interest ahead of the issue and should not be interpreted as confirmed allotments.
Jio's Business Extends Beyond Telecommunications
Jio Platforms has expanded beyond mobile connectivity into a broader portfolio of digital services. Its business interests include broadband, cloud services, entertainment and enterprise solutions, alongside its telecommunications operations.
This wider business presence is expected to be an important consideration for investors assessing the company’s growth prospects and valuation.
The proposed listing would allow the market to determine a separate valuation for Jio Platforms, which currently sits within the Reliance Industries group. Investors would be able to buy shares in the digital services business directly rather than gaining exposure to it indirectly through Reliance Industries shares.
The company's ability to grow its subscriber base, expand digital services and generate revenue across different business segments will be among the factors investors may consider when evaluating the offering.
IPO Timeline And Pricing Details
The information provided alongside the report lists an indicative price band of Rs 1,065 to Rs 1,119 per share, with the IPO scheduled to open on October 21 and close on October 23.
These details indicate a three-day subscription window for investors to participate in the issue. The price band and dates should be verified against the final offer documents and official announcements before publication, as they are not independently confirmed by the cited report in the supplied material.
The proposed offering is expected to bring Jio Platforms into the listed market as a standalone company, creating a new investment avenue for retail and institutional investors.
While the reported demand of nearly Rs 2.5 lakh crore highlights the level of interest ahead of the IPO, the final subscription figures, allocation details and listing performance will provide a clearer picture of investor participation.
For prospective investors, the company's business fundamentals, valuation, financial performance and risk factors will remain important considerations alongside the reported institutional interest.

articles.summary: IMF Expects Kazakhstan’s Inflation to Ease and Economic Growth to Accelerate in 2027  The Astana Times
articles.full_text:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan’s inflation is projected to decline to 8.2% in 2027, while economic growth is expected to accelerate to 4.9%, according to the International Monetary Fund’s (IMF) latest World Economic Outlook, released Oct. 13 at the IMF and World Bank annual meetings in Bangkok.
The IMF forecasts inflation to fall from 11.4% in 2025 to 10.3% in 2026 before declining further next year. Economic growth is projected at 4.4% in 2026, rising to 4.9% in 2027.
The report also identifies Kazakhstan among the countries outside the Persian Gulf that increased oil production and helped the global market adjust to disruptions in supplies through the Strait of Hormuz.
Kazakhstan’s economic outlook
The IMF expects Kazakhstan’s unemployment rate to remain at 4.6% in 2026 before easing to 4.5% in 2027. The country’s current account balance is projected to remain positive at 0.5% of gross domestic product in 2026.
Kazakhstan is also mentioned in the report’s assessment of the economic effects of the artificial intelligence boom. The fund identifies the country among commodity exporters benefiting from increased exports of technology-related goods produced by major Asian manufacturing economies.
Oil supply and the Strait of Hormuz
The report examines how the conflict in the Middle East disrupted global energy markets, with supplies through the Strait of Hormuz nearly halted in the spring. The disruption affected a route responsible for approximately 20% of global oil supplies, pushing prices to $126 per barrel in late March, according to the information cited in the report.
The IMF said the market adapted partly because countries outside the Persian Gulf increased production. Brazil, Kazakhstan, the United States and Venezuela were among those identified as helping offset the supply shortfall.
The report’s global outlook remains closely tied to developments in the Middle East. The IMF assumes that the Strait of Hormuz will reopen in March 2027 and that shipping will return to previous levels by October 2027. Under this scenario, oil prices are projected to average $96 per barrel in 2026 and $87 in 2027.
Artificial intelligence supports global growth
The IMF raised its forecast for global economic growth in 2026 to 3.1%, up from 3% in its July projection. The global economy grew by 3.5% in 2025, while growth is expected to reach 3.4% in 2027.
The fund attributes the improved outlook partly to substantial investment in artificial intelligence infrastructure, which is helping offset the economic effects of higher energy prices and the prolonged conflict in the Middle East.
Economies building AI platforms and manufacturing the equipment needed to support them are among those receiving upgraded forecasts. The report highlights South Korea, Malaysia, Mexico and Thailand in this context.
According to Reuters, Petya Koeva Brooks, deputy director of the IMF’s Research Department, said the global economy would have grown more slowly in 2026 without measures taken by governments and businesses following the oil shock. These included drawing on inventories, finding alternative suppliers and reducing oil consumption.
However, the IMF cautions that the effects of these adjustments are weakening as the conflict continues.
The benefits of AI-related investment are also becoming increasingly concentrated. According to the report’s assessment cited by Reuters, 32 countries now account for 95% of global growth, compared with 54 countries in April. Since then, the IMF has downgraded its growth forecasts for 47% of the world’s economies.
Diverging growth prospects
The United States is projected to grow by 2.3% in both 2026 and 2027, supported by consumer spending, tax cuts and investment in AI. The IMF raised its 2026 growth forecast for the euro area from 0.9% to 1.1% and expects the United Kingdom’s economy to expand by 1.3%. Investment in AI is among the factors supporting these projections, alongside higher defense spending in Europe.
China’s economy is projected to grow by 4.5% in 2026 and 4% in 2027. Higher oil prices are weighing on domestic demand, although strong exports continue to provide support. India is expected to remain the fastest-growing major economy, with projected growth of 7% annually.
By contrast, the Middle East’s oil-producing economies face significant pressure. The IMF forecasts Saudi Arabia’s economy to contract by 3.3% in 2026, reversing its July projection of 1.7% growth. The fund also expects deep economic contractions in Iran, Iraq, Kuwait, Qatar and the United Arab Emirates.
Inflation and risks to the global outlook
Global inflation is projected to reach 4.7% in 2026 before easing to 4.1% in 2027. However, the outlook depends heavily on how the conflict in the Middle East develops and whether energy supplies recover as anticipated.
The IMF also highlights uncertainty surrounding AI investment. Faster adoption of the technology could add 0.6% to global gross domestic product by 2029. Conversely, if the expected productivity gains fail to materialize and investment falls sharply, global economic output could be 1.1% lower by 2028, with the United States facing a potential decline of 1.8%.
High public debt, particularly in advanced economies, presents another challenge. The IMF urges governments to rebuild fiscal buffers and establish credible plans to return public debt to sustainable levels.
“The global economy has proved resilient, but this resilience is reaching its limits, so we need to move from simply surviving to rebuilding,” the IMF’s chief economist, Silvana Tenreyro, said, according to Reuters.

| Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh at a press conference following the FOMC meeting on June 17, 2026. Photo: Federal Reserve/Public domain. | 
 Failure to predict policy decisions
 Speaking at the annual meeting of the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and the World Bank (WB) in Bangkok, Thailand on October 16, US Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh expressed optimism about the resilience of the US economy, while noting that the global economy is demonstrating better-than-expected adaptability to energy shocks and tightening monetary policy. However, he did not give any specific indication of whether the Fed might need to raise interest rates further, or if so, when.
 “I’m not predicting the outcome of the meetings,” Warsh said during a conversation with International Monetary Fund (IMF) Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva, adding: “I don’t believe it’s possible to say at this point what I might do at the remaining meetings this year.”
 This stance continues to reflect Warsh's style of governance since assuming the Fed chairmanship in May 2026. Instead of making commitments on an interest rate path, he focuses on the economic outlook and demands assurances of price stability.
 Referring to the September interest rate hike, Mr. Warsh emphasized that the Fed had clearly demonstrated its determination to maintain price stability and to partially withdraw its supportive monetary policy. Last month, the Fed raised interest rates by 25 basis points, bringing the policy interest rate range to 3.75–4.00%.
 According to Mr. Warsh, inflation is not just a challenge for the United States. Through discussions with central bank leaders in Bangkok, he found that rising prices are becoming a common concern. This has led many central banks to simultaneously tighten monetary policy in order to control inflation.
 Notably, the Fed chairman's remarks came shortly after the latest reports showed that US consumer inflation and producer prices both rose more sharply than expected in September, raising concerns about the possibility of continued price pressures. However, the fact that Mr. Warsh did not signal an interest rate hike in October helped maintain expectations that the Fed would temporarily keep its policy unchanged at the October 27-28 meeting.
 The market is leaning towards the possibility of an interest rate hike in December.
 Meanwhile, many Fed officials have recently publicly stated their views on the interest rate outlook. Accordingly, a significant number of officials believe that the Fed may need to continue tightening policy, but want to wait for more data to assess inflation trends before making a decision. This reinforces the possibility that the Fed will not raise interest rates a second time in October.
 Investors have reduced their bets on the likelihood of the Fed raising interest rates at its policy meeting on October 27-28. The probability of the Fed raising rates at this meeting – which hovered around 27% before Mr. Warsh's remarks – fell below 15% after his comments.
 According to CME Group's FedWatch tool, the market currently prices a 90% probability of the Fed raising interest rates in December, suggesting that investors still believe inflationary pressures will force the US central bank to continue acting, even if the timing of the rate hike is delayed.
 Meanwhile, on October 16, Barclays adjusted its forecast for US monetary policy, suggesting that the Fed will raise interest rates by another 25 basis points in December 2026 and another 25 basis points in January 2027, following better-than-expected inflation figures. Previously, the bank had only forecast one interest rate hike in December.
 Another noteworthy point in Mr. Warsh's speech was the impact of the wave of AI investment on the economy. According to the Fed Chairman, initial investment focused on AI is spreading to many other sectors, creating additional growth momentum but also boosting demand and putting pressure on prices in the short term.
 Mr. Warsh expressed optimism about the impact of AI on economic growth and productivity in the medium term, although he acknowledged that realizing productivity improvements in the "real economy," thereby increasing wealth, will be a "very bumpy" road.
 “Clearly, AI is impacting the demand side of the economy before it impacts the supply side,” he said. “We don’t know how AI will affect jobs in the next 12 or 18 months. But if you, like me, believe that AI will help economies and countries that leverage it become more productive, thereby creating more wealth, then that must certainly be a very positive thing.”
 The Fed chairman also said a working group has been established to advise the Fed on the impact of AI on productivity and jobs, and is expected to hold a “field hearing” in the San Francisco Bay Area on November 16. This will be the first time the public has had access to the work of this group.
 The Fed's policy dilemma is becoming more complex: economic growth still has supporting drivers, while inflation has not yet returned to the 2% target. Therefore, the Fed Chairman's lack of a signal about a decision in October does not mean the likelihood of further tightening has decreased. Instead, the market is becoming more discerning between when the Fed might raise interest rates again and the degree of tightening needed in the coming months.

When interest rates go up, that tends to be bad news for stocks. But not all stocks are affected the same way by rising rates. At their most recent meeting of the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) on Sept. 16, the central bankers hiked the benchmark federal funds rate by 0.25 percentage points. Inflation in September came in slightly hotter than expected, with a year-over-year CPI increase of 3.7%. That suggests that the Fed might hike rates again in 2026, as the FOMC will meet two more times this year, on Oct. 28 and Dec. 9.
When the Fed hikes interest rates, its goal is often to slow inflation -- and tap the brakes on economic growth. This can have negative effects on job growth, borrowing costs, and consumer spending. Some retail stocks might suffer more from a consumer spending slowdown than others. A few important retail stocks to watch right now are Costco (COST +1.14%), Home Depot (HD +0.45%), Target (TGT -1.51%), and Walmart (WMT +0.80%).
Here's how these four retail stocks have performed since the federal funds rate hike on Sept. 16:
A 25-basis-point rate hike is unlikely to be a game changer for any stock. But some companies are more rate-sensitive than others. All four of these retailers have distinct strengths and vulnerabilities that would come into play in a rising interest-rate environment.
Let's look at which of these retail stocks are more likely to be winners if the Fed hikes interest rates again in 2026, and which might be losers.
Costco: Affluent consumers unfazed by higher gas prices
Costco might be better positioned than most retailers to thrive in an environment of higher inflation and rising interest rates. That's because Costco's membership model creates a high level of customer loyalty, and the retailer tends to be popular with higher-income customers. According to a June YouGov survey, 11% of Americans in households with gross incomes of $150,000 or more do most of their food and other grocery shopping at Costco. These more affluent households are likely to be less bothered by high inflation.
A major factor in the Fed hiking interest rates is inflation driven by higher gas prices. The latest CPI index for gasoline was up 9.1% year over year in September 2026. Higher gas prices could hurt some retailers more than others, as consumers are compelled to dedicate more of their take-home pay to filling their tanks.
But Costco might be relatively safe from the effects of high gas prices. As of 2025, about 10% of its total net sales came from gasoline. In the company's September quarterly earnings report, CEO Ron Vachris said Costco's gasoline business had a "record year" and that in its fiscal year 2026, it achieved an all-time high rate of "penetration of U.S. member households that purchased gas."
Costco stock has gained about 118% in the past five years, but over the past year, it underperformed the S&P 500 index (^GSPC -1.09%), rising only 3.75%.
Key data points
Verdict: Bullish. Costco is likely to be a relatively strong retail performer, even with additional Fed rate hikes.
Home Depot: Vulnerable to a sluggish housing market and consumer credit
Fed rate hikes don't directly affect mortgage rates, which are tied to the yield on the 10-year Treasury bond. But the fact that the Fed is hiking short-term interest rates will likely be reflected in higher bond yields on longer-term debt as well. That means more expensive mortgages, more expensive consumer credit, fewer people taking out home loans and home equity loans -- and less money being spent at home improvement stores like Home Depot.
Home Depot's stock price has declined by about 14.1% over the past five years and by about 24% over the past year. And if interest rates stay high or rise, it is probably going to stay in a slump. With higher mortgage rates and a struggling housing market, fewer people are going to spend big on new kitchens and bathrooms.
Key data points
Verdict: Bearish. Until interest rates decline and the housing market gets unstuck, Home Depot shares are likely to keep going sideways -- or worse.
Target: Price-sensitive consumers could threaten this company's turnaround
Target CEO Michael Fiddelke started his job on Feb. 1, and he's tasked with turning the chain around after years of sluggish sales and declining share prices. Fiddelke's plan focuses on refreshing Target's stores and improving its merchandise. So far, it seems to be working: The company's stock is up about 59% year to date.
Key data points
But continued high inflation could be a bigger threat to Target than to Costco. Although Target cut prices on thousands of items in 2026, its customer base could be less loyal than Costco's and more prone to trade down to lower-priced merchandise -- or switch to competitors like Walmart that might be perceived as lower cost.
Verdict: Bearish. One or two Fed rate hikes won't unravel Target's turnaround. But if inflation-weary consumers get more aggressive about bargain hunting, that could be bad news for this "cheap chic" retailer.
Walmart: Opportunity to attract more high-income customers
America's largest retailer is known for low prices. Walmart's customer base tends to be middle-income and lower-income shoppers who want value for their money. Unfortunately, those customers seem to be struggling due to high inflation.
On its most recent quarterly earnings call on Aug. 20, Walmart reported U.S. comparable sales growth of 2.6%, which was weaker than analysts had expected. The company's shares gained an impressive 149% over the past five years, but only 8.4% in the past year -- less than the S&P 500.
But if the Fed keeps hiking interest rates in its bid to bring inflation back in check, there could also be an opportunity for Walmart to expand its market share among more affluent households. On the Aug. 20 earnings call, Walmart CEO John Furner said that "we continue to see growth from higher-income households." If more affluent consumers get fed up with high prices at their usual stores and start to "trade down" to Walmart, that could be good news for this company's investors.
Verdict: Bullish. But only if Walmart can attract more sales from price-sensitive affluent shoppers "trading down" than it loses from lower-income customers who cut back on shopping altogether.

articles.title: Semiconductor correction: reality check after strong rally - ABN Amro
articles.summary: Semiconductor correction: reality check after strong rally  ABN Amro
articles.full_text:
Semiconductor stocks have come under significant pressure in recent days. However, the correction follows an exceptional rally. Even after this week’s decline, the MSCI Semiconductor index[1] remains around 45% higher year-to-date, although it is now more than 10% below its 2026 high. So far, this looks more like a reset in expectations than evidence of a fundamental deterioration in the semiconductor cycle or underlying AI demand.
What are the main reasons for the sharp downturn in semiconductor stocks? Several concerns have converged at the same time. First, AI returns and financing are increasingly becoming central concerns. Investors wonder whether the enormous capital committed to AI infrastructure will generate sufficient returns. Higher interest rates make this more challenging, as they lead to higher financing costs for investments in data centres and computing capacity.
In credit markets, investors also increasingly worry about financing risks related to AI. CoreWeave, one of the more highly leveraged AI infrastructure providers, has seen the cost of insuring its debt against default rise sharply (much higher spreads on credit default swaps). In other words, credit investors are demanding much more compensation for the risk of lending to the company. If financing becomes structurally more expensive, highly leveraged AI companies may have to moderate their data centre expansion and, ultimately, chip purchases. The cost of insuring against defaults by other AI-related companies has also increased.
Safety of AI called into question
AI safety is emerging as another potential constraint. The rise of ‘agentic AI’ – AI systems that can autonomously plan and carry out tasks – raises concerns around cybersecurity, liability and regulation. Anthropic, the company behind chatbot Claude, recently warned that autonomous AI agents could become increasingly difficult to control. Tighter safeguards are unlikely to stop AI development, but they could slow the rollout of commercial applications and delay returns, meaning current AI investments could take longer to pay off.
Competition from China
Chinese competition is amplifying the correction. Advances by semiconductor company CXMT, a Chinese rival of other memory chip makers, have raised concerns over future memory chip supply and competition. If supply increases faster than formerly expected, memory chip prices could fall quicker, putting pressure on manufacturers’ margins and profits.
Finally, the upcoming US midterm elections could add another layer of uncertainty. Political scrutiny of the rapid expansion of datacentres is increasing, particularly because of their energy use and the pressure they place on existing infrastructure. While unlikely to derail the AI build-out altogether, this could result in permitting delays, higher costs or a slower pace of capacity expansion.
Positive view, but more clarity needed
Still, there is little evidence of a fundamental deterioration in demand for semiconductors. This week, ASML mentioned its currently planned capacity will not be sufficient to meet customer demand in 2027 and 2028. This indicates that demand for AI-related chips remains strong in the near and medium term. Beyond 2028, demand is more uncertain. For demand to remain strong after 2028, today's enormous AI investments will have to translate into sufficient revenues and returns.
Be selective and monitor developments
For now, we see the correction in semiconductor stocks as a reset in expectations rather than the start of a downturn: in some areas, expectations of sustained, exceptionally high growth are being revised. For investors, however, this does not make every correction a buying opportunity. After the strong rally that preceded the correction, selectivity matters more.
We favour semiconductor companies with a strong order outlook , strategic positions in the semiconductor value chain and robust balance sheets. We are more cautious towards businesses that heavily depend on continued rapid growth in AI investment, as the focus of investors is increasingly shifting from AI investment to AI returns. Evidence that AI revenues are catching up with AI infrastructure spending would strengthen the case that today’s expansion in semiconductor capacity can be sustained well beyond 2028. Conversely, if AI generates lower profits than expected, financing costs remain persistently high, or material cuts are made to data centre investment, the risk of overcapacity and a weaker semiconductor investment cycle later in the decade would increase.
Our conclusion is therefore not to abandon the semiconductor theme, but to be more selective. The 2027-28 outlook remains strong; the case for growth beyond 2028 has yet to be proven.
Conclusion
OpenAI, Anthropic and DeepSeek are not simply preparing for their IPOs. They are also helping define how equity markets will value AI. While all three require substantial capital to fuel growth, they represent very different visions of AI's future: a global consumer platform, a premium provider of corporate AI solutions, and an efficiency-driven challenger from China.
Their eventual market debuts will be more than financing events. They will serve as a crucial test of investor confidence in the long-term economics of AI and could shape market sentiment, valuations and capital flows across the entire AI sector for years to come. The first successful frontier AI IPO may ultimately become the moment when AI evolves from a technology trend into a fully established asset class for (public) equity investors.
Joost Olde Riekerink
Equity Research & Advisory Expert

In Mexico, rating agency HR Ratings on October 15, 2026, downgraded the global credit rating of state oil company Pemex from HR BBB+ to HR BBB. The rating outlook remained stable. As The Rio Times reports, the decision was made on the same day the agency downgraded Mexico’s sovereign rating to HR BBB.
Link to the state rating
HR Ratings views Pemex as a company with de facto sovereign status, as the Mexican government provides it with funds for debt servicing, capital expenditures and fiscal support. The agency also noted that Pemex is an important source of revenue for the country. Therefore, the change in Mexico’s sovereign rating directly affected the assessment of the company’s creditworthiness.
According to the publication, the downgrade of the global rating applies to 25 Pemex debt issues. At the same time, the agency affirmed the company’s local ratings at HR AAA and HR+1 with stable outlooks. The HR BBB rating on the HR Ratings scale still belongs to the investment-grade category.
More current news is available on the UA.News Telegram channel Telegram.
Debt and financial indicators
Pemex’s total debt as of the end of June 2026 stood at 1.353 trillion pesos, or about $77.5 billion. This is 11.6% lower than at the end of 2025 in peso terms and 9.1% lower in dollar terms. HR Ratings attributes the reduction primarily to debt repayments financed by contributions from the federal government.
In the first half of 2026, Pemex’s revenue increased by 11.3% to 876 billion pesos. The growth was driven by a 17.4% increase in domestic sales and higher reference prices. Production of oil and other liquid hydrocarbons averaged 1.655 million barrels per day in the second quarter, 2% more than a year earlier.
HR Ratings forecasts that Pemex’s net debt will decrease to 1.298 trillion pesos in 2026 and to 1.250 trillion pesos in 2028. This forecast assumes continued refinancing and financial support from the federal government.

articles.full_text:
US Federal Reserve boss Kevin Warsh said Friday the global economy had shown unexpected resilience against strong economic shocks, as central banks battle surging inflation, while rich countries tackle spiking bond yields.
"Almost everywhere in the global economy (is) showing resilience I'm not sure I would have predicted five or six months ago," he told an event hosted by IMF chief Kristalina Georgieva at the IMF-World Bank Annual Meetings in Bangkok.
World energy prices have skyrocketed since US President Donald Trump launched the war on Iran in February, sparking retaliatory action by Tehran against Washington's Gulf allies and plunging the Middle East into crisis.
The increase in oil and gas costs, along with a surge in AI investments, has spurred inflation in many economies, including the United States, putting pressure on central banks to raise interest rates.
While many other rich economies were able to bring post-pandemic inflation back to their targets, the Fed has failed to meet its long-term two-percent goal for more than five years.
Since taking over as Fed chair in May, Warsh has promised the central bank will deliver on its price stability commitment, and in September it raised rates for the first time in three years.
The Fed meets again this month to set rates, and markets expect it to hold before a second 25-basis-point hike in December.
Warsh has vowed to cut down on providing insights into Fed policy positions, and on Friday again refrained from sharing his view of what may transpire at the October gathering.
"We came to a judgement" about the economic outlook at the September meeting, he said. "I want to say broadly over the month or so that's transpired since then, the world has broadly conformed to our expectations."
- 'Common challenges' -
The annual meetings bring together finance ministers, central bankers and policymakers from around the world, and Warsh said he had heard from others of the "common challenges" advanced economies faced.
"I heard, I would say, resolve from my colleagues around the world to deliver price stability," he said.
Most rich nations have begun to raise rates in response to surging inflation, including the European Central Bank (ECB).
"If I look back over the last few months, while we each did the right thing by our own judgement, by our own remit, it was a synchronous tightening in monetary policy in most places around the world," said Warsh.
"And that means there's no free riders. We're seeing common things, and we're taking action, and I view that as a positive development."

articles.title: Bad Inflation Cures Itself. Good Inflation Doesn't - RIA - Real Investment Advice
articles.summary: Bad Inflation Cures Itself. Good Inflation Doesn't - RIA  Real Investment Advice
articles.full_text:
The economy is running bad inflation, and the bad kind is the temporary kind, which is precisely why the bond market refuses to panic.
Most of the argument about inflation right now is a fight between people using the same word for two completely different things. One side sees a 3.7% headline print and starts sketching a repeat of 1979. The other sees core running more than a point below it and declares the problem solved. Both are reading the same release. The distinction that matters is not how big the number is, but whether anybody’s income is financing it. That is the line between “good” inflation and bad inflation, and almost nobody draws it.
Good Inflation, Bad Inflation, And The Difference Nobody Makes
There is a general framework to inflation, and it is older than any of us. Prices can rise because buyers are bidding for scarce goods with money they’ve actually earned. Or prices can rise because the cost of producing something has jumped for reasons unrelated to demand. An oil embargo will do it, as we saw in the 1970s. So does a shuttered Strait of Hormuz, a new tariff schedule, or a pandemic that takes half the world’s shipping capacity offline for eighteen months.
This is an important point for the “debasement” crowd, whose narrative overlooks the underlying fundamentals.
“The following economic illustration is taught in every ‘Econ 101’ class. Unsurprisingly, inflation is the consequence if supply is restricted and demand increases via monetary interventions.”
However, there is a very important distinction to be made about inflation. The first type is the “good” kind of inflation, and it is genuinely good. Demand pushes prices up; firms book wider margins; tight labor markets funnel those margins into paychecks, and the higher paychecks fund the higher prices. The loop closes and becomes self-reinforcing because every leg of it is paid for by real output.
The second kind, the “bad” kind of inflation, closes nothing. A tariff is a tax, just like an oil shock is a tax. Somebody’s cost went up, and the money has to come out of a budget that did not grow. Every dollar of that price increase is a dollar not spent somewhere else. Bad inflation doesn’t create the income that pays for it, so it destroys the demand that supports it. Such is the mechanism behind the oldest saying in commodities: “high prices cure high prices.”
Think of it this way. A group of people drives the same way to work every day. Half get a raise, the other half doesn’t. The city decides to put a toll booth on the road they drive to work; each year, that toll rises. Both groups have an increasing number draining their bank accounts each month. However, only one group has sufficient compensation to continue using the toll road. The group without the compensation raise is eventually forced to stop using the toll road; traffic falls, and the operator cuts the toll to win them back.
What The September Print Actually Says
Let’s review the recent August data to see what the message, versus the narrative, actually is. The headline CPI came in at 3.7% year over year in September. Core came in at 2.6%, a tick higher than August. Read that pair again, because it is the whole argument. The gap between them widened from nine-tenths of a point to one and a tenth, meaning the headline accelerated roughly three times faster than the core.
That gap suggests a very different narrative than what the media suggests. Gasoline rose 9.1% in the month alone and 34.2% over the year, and the BLS attributes over half the entire monthly increase in the all-items index to that one category. Energy overall is up 20.4%. Meanwhile, core goods, where a genuine demand boom would show up first and loudest, rose 0.7% over twelve months, sitting exactly where it was in August. Shelter ticked up to 3.2%
Now the part I owe you, because I set a test in advance. Core ticked up, shelter ticked up, and services’ less energy reached 3.1%, which would eventually prove me wrong. One month of tenths is noise rather than a trend. It is also the first month this year that those three moved the wrong way together, and core goods holding flat at 0.7% is why I am not moving yet, because that is where a demand boom announces itself first, and it has not.
Headline CPI pulled further away from core in September. The shaded area is the spread, and the spread is energy. Source: BLS via Massive Market Data, September 2026.
I’ve been making this argument since June, when I wrote about why the May 4.2% headline was an oil story rather than a demand story. To wit:
“A 4.2% headline that is three-fifths gasoline is not the same animal as a 4.2% headline driven by wages, rents, and services broadening.”
Four months later, the composition has not changed. What has changed is that the evidence against the demand-pull story got considerably stronger.
Labor Just Set A 79-Year Low
The most important evidence comes from the labor market. If this were the “good” kind of inflation, workers would be capturing some of it. They are not.
Real average hourly earnings fell 0.7% over the twelve months through September, more than double the August decline. Nominal wages rose 0.1% on the month against a 0.6% CPI print, so purchasing power went backward at the fastest pace of the year. Run the same calculation off average hourly earnings and CPI, and you land in the same place. Real wage growth is near -0.7%, down from over 1.5% as recently as last spring.
In April 2026, real wage growth crossed below zero and hit its weakest reading in September. The gold bars represent the months when wages grew faster than prices. The red bars are months when they didn’t. Source: BLS via Massive Market Data, August 2026.
Then there is the one number that everyone simply overlooked. In the second quarter, labor’s share of nonfarm business output fell to 52.8%. The Bureau of Labor Statistics flagged that as the lowest level in a series that begins in the first quarter of 1947. Read that again. There have been 79 years of data, 2 dozen business cycles, 4 major wars, the Volcker shock, the China trade shock, and the pandemic. Despite all that, in what is supposed to be an economic boom, we just set a record low.
Here is what it looks like graphically. This is not what an inflationary boom looks like.
Labor’s share of output has been falling for a quarter century and just made a series low. Good inflation requires this line to rise. Source: BLS, Productivity and Costs, Q2 2026.
Stop and notice that in the chart above, this is not a 2026 event. The erosion in labor runs back to the early 2000s, long before “artificial intelligence” or “surging debt.” The last two years have simply accelerated the numbers. With respect to the inflation question, the timing matters most. A price level that is rising while labor’s slice of output hits an all-time low is the textbook signature of cost pass-through rather than demand-pull. In this environment, corporations are fixated on protecting profit margins, while workers are absorbing the difference.
The economic activity surveys tell the same story if you take the time to read past the headlines. The ISM services printed 54.9 in September, with new orders easing to 59.8. That reads like a demand boom until you see prices paid at 74.0, the highest since July 2022, while the employment index has not exceeded 50.1 in three months. Steady orders, hot input costs, flat payrolls. When respondents were asked what was driving those costs, fuel came up about twice as often as anything else.
Where The Inflation Bulls Have A Point
As always, we need to examine both sides of every argument, as the inflation bulls do have a valid point.
The strongest one is the AI buildout. Memory is genuinely scarce; its scarcity is genuinely caused by capital spending, and the producer price index for storage devices has climbed 23% since the end of 2024, while import prices for computers and parts are up 37%. J.P. Morgan’s research team puts the memory shock at 0.2% to 0.4% on core inflation. That is capex-driven price pressure; it is real, and it did not come from an embargo. However, that scarcity will eventually reverse. As with oil prices, high prices eventually curtail demand.
The second argument is that tariffs are a policy choice, not a weather event. That is a true statement, and a tariff regime that stays in place for years produces a price level that stays elevated for years. Calling that “transitory” is a semantic trick. I can’t argue with that. A permanent tax produces a permanent price. However, the current tariffs were not enacted by Congressional legislation, which would make them more permanent. In this case, they were enacted through executive order, which means the next Administration can repeal them quickly.
The third is that energy is not reliably mean-reverting on any schedule you can trade. Geopolitics doesn’t run on a calendar. However, high oil prices, as shown in the chart below, reliably mean-revert over time.
Those are all sound and valid arguments, but there is a problem with all three, though. Every one of them describes a SUPPLY constraint. A memory shortage is, by definition, a shortage. Call the tariff what it is: a tax. And the Middle East risk is a supply risk. None of them creates the income that pays the higher price. All three fail the same test: gasoline fails, and a more flattering story doesn’t change what the bill does to a household budget.
Why Bad Inflation Cures Itself
“Inflation is inflation. My grocery bill doesn’t care about the taxonomy.”
That is a fair statement. The pain from inflation is the same either way, and when you are staring at the number on the gas pump, the squeeze on household budgets happens regardless. Just because it happens to be the academically preferable kind, the household budget just doesn’t care. However, the taxonomy isn’t about how it feels, but how it ends, and bad inflation ends in a way the good kind never does.

articles.title: Ailing Shilling forces BoU into emergency policy tightening amid $200m capital flight - Daily Monitor
articles.summary: Ailing Shilling forces BoU into emergency policy tightening amid $200m capital flight  Daily Monitor
articles.full_text:
The Bank of Uganda (BoU) has returned to direct intervention in the foreign exchange market for the first time since June 2022, selling approximately $30 million (Shs120 billion) late on Wednesday in an aggressive bid to arrest the local currency's slide past the psychological Shs4,000 threshold against the US dollar.
The direct market sale capped a dramatic week in which the central bank was forced to convene an emergency Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) meeting and deliver its largest benchmark interest rate increase in 15 years.
In his weekly market assessment, Mr. Stephen Kaboyo, Partner at Alpha Capital and forex market analyst, noted that the local unit experienced significant volatility following BoU’s multi-pronged approach.
"Uganda Shilling experienced major shifts after the BoU stepped in with a hike in the benchmark rate following an emergency Monetary Policy meeting. In a multi-pronged approach, the Central Bank, in a surprise move, also intervened in the market, an action last seen in June 2022 by selling about 30 million dollars (Shs120 billion) late on Wednesday. The move triggered a strong rebound, driving the shilling back below the 4000 threshold. However, in subsequent market sessions, the currency surrendered its short-lived gains," Mr. Kaboyo said.
Looking ahead, Mr. Kaboyo warned that market fundamentals remain fragile. "In the coming days, the outlook indicates that underlying pressures remain intact. The shilling will continue facing persistent downward market forces that will keep it on the back foot, with the primary driver being the substantial outstanding exposure of portfolio investors to the local bond market. The unpredictable nature of these flows will keep the unit on the edge," he added.
The central bank's intervention briefly halted eight consecutive sessions of losses after the currency hit a record low of Shs4,143 per dollar—its weakest level since 1993, making it the worst-performing currency among 144 tracked globally by Bloomberg this month. Data from LSEG showed the shilling temporarily gaining over 2 percent on the day following the action.
In an official statement detailing the outcomes of the special MPC meeting held on October 14, 2026, BoU Governor Dr. Michael Atingi-Ego announced a dramatic 225-basis-point increase in the Central Bank Rate (CBR), lifting it from 9.75 percent to 12.0 percent. The hike represents the largest monthly increase since October 2011 and elevates the benchmark rate to its highest level since December 2016, ending a two-year period of unchanged monetary policy. Additionally, the central bank raised the Cash Reserve Requirement (CRR) for commercial banks from 11.0 percent to 13.5 percent, effective September 24.
The central bank linked the drastic tightening to heightened Middle East geopolitical conflicts, surging global energy prices, and tighter international financial conditions. These external headwinds expanded Uganda's current account deficit by $1.4 billion (Shs5.6 trillion) to a total of $4.6 billion (Shs18.4 trillion), while headline inflation accelerated to 4.6 percent in September up from 4.1 percent in August.
Adding to the liquidity strain, estimates from Citigroup reveal that over $200 million (Shs799.8 billion) exited Uganda's domestic market in just two weeks as offshore investors reallocated capital from local government bonds into higher-yielding US dollar assets.
Introduced in July 2011 at 13 percent under BoU's Inflation Targeting Lite framework, the CBR serves as a key signal for the cost of money and aims to anchor core inflation around 5 percent.
The policy rate reached a historic peak of 23 percent in November 2011 when inflation approached 30 percent, before gradually easing to 9.5 percent by October 2017. During the COVID-19 pandemic in June 2021, the rate hit an all-time low of 6.5 percent to stimulate economic activity. Prior to the latest decision, the rate was last raised during an emergency meeting in July 2022 to 8.5 percent and had remained steady at 9.75 percent since October 2024.
Financial experts and economists remain divided on whether monetary tightening is the effective remedy for current market conditions.
Mr. Uthman Mayanja, Country Senior Partner at PwC Uganda, explained that the central bank's primary objective is mitigating imported inflation pressures.
"The Bank of Uganda's decision is about controlling inflation. As the shilling weakens, imports such as fuel and machinery become more expensive. Eventually, this drives prices for consumer goods higher. The typical response is to raise interest rates to make saving more attractive and borrowing more expensive, thereby easing pressure on prices. In turn, higher interest rates strengthen local and international demand for Ugandan treasury bills and bonds, which should reduce pressure on the Shilling. In short, the Bank is tightening money supply today to contain inflation risks from a weaker shilling, while also making shilling-denominated investments more attractive," Mr. Mayanja noted.
Conversely, Dr. Fred Muhumuza, a senior economist at Makerere University, argued that hiking interest rates is an inadequate solution for external supply-side shocks.
"The central bank is trying to also tell people to think twice before you borrow," Dr. Muhumuza stated, pointing out that "BoU is emphasising the message of risk aversion, but to even tell them that this is not a risk, it is a reality…that is the space we are in." He maintained that raising domestic interest rates cannot resolve imported fuel price inflation or structural foreign exchange shortages.
Adding to these concerns, Dr. Susan Kavuma warned that commercial banks will rapidly transmit the higher central bank rate to end-user borrowing costs, severely dampening private sector credit growth. She highlighted that Uganda’s average lending rate of 17.3 percent recorded in July was already higher than neighboring regional peers like Kenya.
Similarly, Ms. Jane Nalunga, Country Director at SEATINI Uganda, cautioned that the ultimate economic burden will fall on vulnerable households and small businesses.
"BoU has raised the CBR by 225 basis points to respond to the record depreciation of the shilling, worsening BoP amid the mounting inflation pressure. It's important to note that this is a remarkable increase marking the end of the 2 years of unchanged rates," Ms. Nalunga said. "While the increase in the CBR intends to curb inflationary pressures and exchange rate depreciation, it comes at a cost."

On the morning of October 16th, local time, at the Queen Sirikit National Convention Center in Bangkok, Thailand , all attention was focused on the conversation between Kevin Warsh, Chairman of the US Federal Reserve (Fed), and Kristalina Georgieva, Managing Director of the International Monetary Fund (IMF).
Global financial circles awaited a clear message about the direction of capital flows ahead of the Fed's executive meeting on October 27-28. However, the response was a decisive stance from the head of the US central bank. According to Reuters, Mr. Warsh stated that he would not make any pre-determined decisions for the upcoming meeting, while remaining silent on the possibility of further interest rate increases or a pause, as generally expected by investors.
"We have made it very clear that we will ensure price stability, and about a month ago we partially scaled back our easing," the Fed chairman said. "I am not predicting the outcome of the Fed meetings. I don't believe in making statements right now about what I can do at the remaining meetings this year," he emphasized.

US Federal Reserve boss Kevin Warsh said Friday the global economy had shown unexpected resilience against strong economic shocks, as central banks battle surging inflation, while rich countries tackle spiking bond yields.
"Almost everywhere in the global economy (is) showing resilience I'm not sure I would have predicted five or six months ago," he told an event hosted by IMF chief Kristalina Georgieva at the IMF-World Bank Annual Meetings in Bangkok.
World energy prices have skyrocketed since US President Donald Trump launched the war on Iran in February, sparking retaliatory action by Tehran against Washington's Gulf allies and plunging the Middle East into crisis.
The increase in oil and gas costs, along with a surge in AI investments, has spurred inflation in many economies, including the United States, putting pressure on central banks to raise interest rates.
While many other rich economies were able to bring post-pandemic inflation back to their targets, the Fed has failed to meet its long-term two-percent goal for more than five years.
Since taking over as Fed chair in May, Warsh has promised the central bank will deliver on its price stability commitment, and in September it raised rates for the first time in three years.
The Fed meets again this month to set rates, and markets expect it to hold before a second 25-basis-point hike in December.
Warsh has vowed to cut down on providing insights into Fed policy positions, and on Friday again refrained from sharing his view of what may transpire at the October gathering.
"We came to a judgement" about the economic outlook at the September meeting, he said. "I want to say broadly over the month or so that's transpired since then, the world has broadly conformed to our expectations."
- 'Common challenges' -
The annual meetings bring together finance ministers, central bankers and policymakers from around the world, and Warsh said he had heard from others of the "common challenges" advanced economies faced.
"I heard, I would say, resolve from my colleagues around the world to deliver price stability," he said.
Most rich nations have begun to raise rates in response to surging inflation, including the European Central Bank (ECB).
"If I look back over the last few months, while we each did the right thing by our own judgement, by our own remit, it was a synchronous tightening in monetary policy in most places around the world," said Warsh.
"And that means there's no free riders. We're seeing common things, and we're taking action, and I view that as a positive development."

ICICI Bank Q2 results
ICICI Bank reported a 20.1% annual jump in standalone net profit to ₹14,843 crore in Q2FY27. The double digit growth was supported by strong loan growth and lower provisions for bad loans.

IDBI Bank Q2 results

articles.title: US corporate lobbyists mounted ‘blitz’ to dilute landmark EU deforestation law, report finds
articles.summary: Environmental watchdog Mighty Earth reveals two-year effort to postpone and weaken EU Deforestation RegulationUS corporate lobbyists launched a two-year “blitz” to postpone and weaken the world’s most progressive legislation to protect forests, according to a new investigation by the environmental watchdog Mighty Earth.Major US firms and trade associations, including Cargill, Bunge, Mondelēz and the US Soybean Export Council, as well as numerous other US firms and organizations, sought to influe...
articles.full_text:
US corporate lobbyists launched a two-year “blitz” to postpone and weaken the world’s most progressive legislation to protect forests, according to a new investigation by the environmental watchdog Mighty Earth.
Major US firms and trade associations, including Cargill, Bunge, Mondelēz and the US Soybean Export Council, as well as numerous other US firms and organizations, sought to influence the EU Deforestation Regulation (EUDR) in more than 350 meetings, the advocacy group found.
US company representatives and industry groups deny there was a concerted campaign to derail the deforestation rules, saying their meetings with EU officials raised legitimate concerns around implementation.
The EUDR prohibits imports of commodities such as cattle, cocoa, coffee, oil palm, rubber, soya and wood from deforested land. When the ban was put forward in 2003, the then European environment commissioner, Virginijus Sinkevičius, described it as “the most ambitious legislative attempt to tackle these issues worldwide ever” and some US lawmakers said it should be a model for similar rules in the United States.
In the years since, its official implementation has been delayed twice and the original goal to rigorously trace the origin of commodities has been revised so much that some of its initial supporters claimed the policy has been in effect “dismantled”. The law will come into effect in December.
Lobbyists from many countries, including Brazil and several EU nations, are known to have contributed to this dilution. Mighty Earth has provided the most detailed analysis yet of the role of organisations from the United States.
It found 24 major US companies, trade associations and industry organizations discussed the EUDR in at least 173 meetings with members of the European parliament and 178 meetings with senior European Commission officials between July 2024 and July 2026.
The US organisations with the highest number of meetings with the European Commission were the National Alliance of Forest Owners, Advanced Woody Biomass Alliance, the US Soybean Export Council, Bunge, the American Chamber of Commerce to the European Union and Cargill.
Cargill had two meetings, Bunge one meeting and Mondlēz eight meetings.
Mighty Earth said lobbying was also conducted through the US Congress, the US Department of Agriculture, the Office of the US Trade Representative and the White House.
Two weeks after a July 2025 meeting at a Scottish golf course between Trump and the president of the European Commission, Ursula von der Leyen, the two sides released a joint statement that promised the US special treatment with regard to the EUDR.
The commission stated the US “poses negligible risk to global deforestation” (even though many of its biggest financial and trading companies have been repeatedly implicated in destruction of the Amazon and similar biomes). The statement also talked about the EU working “to address the concerns of US producers and exporters regarding EUDR, with a view to avoiding undue impact on US-EU trade”.
Mighty Earth said its investigation highlighted the need for the EU to adopt greater transparency about lobbying activities and to give more access to civil society to ensure balance.
“Our analysis found a relentless and aggressive campaign by major US businesses, trade bodies and government officials, going all the way to President Trump, who offered to personally intervene, to further pressure EU policymakers,” Isabel Fernandez, senior adviser for Mighty Earth, said. “Some of the companies lobbying the EU, include the most egregious who are still linked to the illegal clearing of forests for commodities, such as soy that make their way into European markets.”
Earlier this year a delegation of Trump administration officials went to EU capitals arguing the law would put the US off exporting to the European market because it would raise costs for US producers. In an opinion piece published in Agence France, Andrew Puzder, the US ambassador to the EU, said the law was: “… sold as a bold strike against global forest loss. In reality it will impose significant regulatory compliance costs while producing inconsequential environmental benefit when enforced against countries that pose no deforestation risk.”
US corporate organisations said their engagement was designed to better understand and enhance the EUDR.
The American Chamber of Commerce to the EU said it had raised concerns about EUDR implementation challenges, such as IT system shortcomings and a lack of clarity around the obligations of companies. But a spokesperson said its role had been constructive: “AmCham EU has consistently supported the EUDR’s objective of tackling global deforestation and promoting sustainable supply chains ... We have asked to allow sufficient time for companies and authorities to prepare and ensure the regulation can be effectively enforced without undermining its environmental objectives.”
The US Soybean Export Council said it was focused on ways to support industry compliance with the EU’s rules. “USSEC does not seek delay or exemption; rather we favour a transition period as the Regulation comes into force. This would allow companies, control authorities, the European Commission, and the entire value chain to gain experience and learnings on how compliance works in practice, allowing for greater understanding and adaptations to implementation if needed moving forwards,” a spokesperson said.
The agribusiness company Bunge said it was committed to deforestation-free supply chains and was investing in monitoring and traceability that had, it said, achieved 100% traceability to farm for both direct and indirect soy sourcing in priority areas of Argentina, Brazil and Paraguay. A spokesperson said: “Bunge supports the objectives of the European Union Deforestation Regulation while observing our own non-deforestation commitment and strengthening responsible sourcing. We are also in contact with relevant EU bodies and national competent authorities via sector organizations and directly to request clarification on certain specific complex scenarios regarding the practical implementation requirements of the EUDR.”
Cargill and Mondelēz did not send an on-the-record response to the Guardian’s request for a comment.

articles.title: Christine Lagarde: IMFC Statement
articles.full_text:
- SPEECH
IMFC Statement
Statement by Christine Lagarde, President of the ECB, at the fifty-fourth meeting of the International Monetary and Financial Committee
IMF Annual Meetings, 17 October 2026
Introduction
The global economy has proven surprisingly resilient in the face of high uncertainty. The conflict in the Middle East continues to expose energy markets to sharp swings. Trade tensions and protectionist measures are weighing on confidence and contributing to a reconfiguration of trade flows. The global economy has held up thanks in part to the rise of artificial intelligence, with investment in technology supporting activity and trade, particularly in economies integrated into technology value chains. Risks nonetheless remain tilted to the downside for growth and to the upside for inflation. A return to an international economic order grounded in openness, predictability and the rule of law would help trade and investment flourish.
Economic activity
Despite global headwinds and the ongoing energy shock, the euro area economy has so far proved resilient. Growth was broad-based across most euro area countries and sectors in the first half of 2026. The September ECB staff projections foresee growth of 0.9% in 2026, 1.4% in 2027 and 1.5% in 2028.
As the energy shock fades over the medium term, the projections see domestic demand benefitting from a recovery in real income over the medium term, driven by lower energy inflation and a resilient labour market. Rising government spending on infrastructure and defence, complemented by investment in AI and digital technologies, should also support growth. Export growth should pick up on the back of strengthening foreign demand, also driven by AI.
The medium-term outlook is surrounded by uncertainty over how intense and long-lasting the Middle East conflict will be, and how the resulting shocks might propagate through the economy. Risks to growth are assessed to be on the downside.
Fiscal sustainability remains a crucial anchor for broader economic stability. It is important to maintain sound fiscal policies, including by adhering to fiscal rules, and, where debt is high, to consolidate, re-prioritise spending and enhance the efficiency and effectiveness of public finances to rebuild buffers. Governments should strive to ensure that any fiscal response to the energy shock is temporary, targeted and tailored.
In addition, policies that strengthen resilience to climate change can improve the economy’s ability to absorb climate-related shocks. These efforts should be complemented by structural policies that promote labour market participation, equip the workforce with the skills needed in an AI-driven economy and facilitate the diffusion of new technologies. Priorities include advancing the savings and investments union, improving access to risk capital and creating better conditions for innovative firms to scale up across the Single Market.
Inflation
Headline inflation increased to 3.8% in September, mostly reflecting a surge in energy inflation, and, to a lesser extent, an increase in food and services inflation. Core inflation increased slightly to 2.5%. The range of underlying inflation measures remained broadly stable in September and wages have so far shown no material response to the energy shock.
Looking ahead, higher energy prices are expected to keep headline inflation well above target into the first half of 2027 and to gradually feed through to core and food inflation. Headline inflation is expected to decline after the first quarter as energy inflation falls, returning to around target towards the end of 2027. The risks to the inflation outlook are to the upside due, in particular, to the Middle East conflict and Russia’s unjustified war against Ukraine. A more intense or persistent energy shock could strengthen indirect and second-round effects, resulting in higher and more persistent inflation. Extreme weather could push up food prices. By contrast, a sustainable resolution of geopolitical conflicts, weaker energy pass-through or more risk-averse financial markets could lower inflation.
Monetary policy
The Governing Council decided to raise the key ECB interest rates by 25 basis points in September, following an increase of the same size in June.
Our interest rate decisions are based on our reaction function, which comprises three criteria: our assessment of the inflation outlook and the risks surrounding it, in light of the incoming economic and financial data, the dynamics of underlying inflation; and the strength of monetary policy transmission.
The inflation outlook points to higher inflation ahead, especially in the short term, given the latest developments in energy markets. However, we see no evidence at this stage of significant pass-through of energy prices to other prices and wages, beyond what we have already included in our projections. And while growth has been resilient, financing conditions have tightened, with long-term interest rates rising notably since our last meeting. This will slow growth and reduce pass-through by more than projected in our September exercise.
Taking these three criteria together, the energy shock is too large to “look through” but a measured response remains appropriate to keep inflation in check.
In setting future policy, we will make a comprehensive assessment of the incoming data based on our reaction function. In July, the Governing Council decided on the operational features and the onboarding process for the enhanced EUREP, the Eurosystem repo facility for central banks that was announced earlier this year. The new facility supports the smooth transmission of monetary policy and reinforces the international role of the euro. More than 30 central banks have expressed interest in EUREP in the past six months.
Financial stability
Sources of risk and vulnerabilities for euro area financial stability remain high. Continued geopolitical tensions, fiscal challenges and uncertainties around accelerated AI adoption continue to be causes for concern. The widespread concentration of critical third-party service providers introduces single points of failure for both financial and non-financial institutions. New frontier AI models have increased cyber risks and operational vulnerabilities.
Euro area banks maintain strong capital and liquidity buffers and robust profitability, together with healthy and stable asset quality. These solid fundamentals should help navigate ongoing geopolitical uncertainties and effectively support lending to the economy. Strengthened prudential regulation and supervision since the global financial crisis has helped leave euro area banks in a strong position to withstand the unfolding economic challenges.
Shocks could expose vulnerabilities among non-bank financial intermediaries, notably from concentrated AI-related exposures, amplifying market stress and creating spillovers across financial sectors. Banks’ exposures to non-banks and vulnerable firms could expose funding and credit vulnerabilities.
Stress in private credit markets has continued, with private credit funds reporting outflows and reactivating redemption gates. Private market “semi-liquid funds” that allow for redemptions are becoming more prevalent, which could lead to greater liquidity mismatches in the future, but euro area financial institutions have limited direct exposure to private credit. This means, for now, that private credit in isolation is unlikely to be a source of financial instability in the euro area.
Payment systems
Central bank money must evolve to fulfil the needs of an increasingly digital economy. The Eurosystem is at the forefront of this evolution, bringing the stability and trust of central bank money to digital retail payments and tokenised finance in Europe. In the retail space we are preparing to complement cash with its digital equivalent – the digital euro – for day-to-day payments. The digital euro will further stimulate innovation and competition in retail payments, ensuring that the continued co-existence of public and private solutions underpins Europe’s strategic autonomy in payments. To lay the groundwork for a seamless and secure launch, we will run a 12-month internal pilot in the second half of 2027. Adopting the Regulation on the establishment of the digital euro by the end of 2026 is key to making this possible.
In the wholesale space, the Eurosystem is developing new capabilities to ensure that central bank money can settle transactions in the growing market of tokenised assets. Pontes – the Eurosystem’s distributed ledger technology (DLT) solution that went live on 21 September – marks the first step in implementing our strategy to enable the development of a European tokenised ecosystem. This vision will be advanced under the Appia initiative, which aims to deliver a blueprint for this ecosystem based on common standards, shared network infrastructure and European governance.
International cooperation
We value the work of our global institutions and fora, particularly those that promote global macroeconomic and financial stability. We welcome the recent completion of the three major IMF reviews (Comprehensive Surveillance Review, Financial Sector Assessment Program Review and Review of Program Design and Conditionality), which strengthen the role of the IMF at the centre of the global financial safety net. Climate-related work should remain fully anchored in IMF operations, particularly surveillance. Multilateral efforts to help tackle global imbalances support coordination of domestic action that is required to minimise the risks from disorderly adjustment. The IMF’s analytical work on global imbalances and its improvements to the methodology for assessing external balances provide a strong basis for these efforts.
